#3707. Destroy All Humans remake developer goes independent, splits from THQ Nordic and parent company Embracer Group

Black Forest Games - the studio that remade the first two cult-classic Destroy All Humans games - has spun out from under former owners THQ Nordic and Embracer Group.

The Destroy All Humans remaker won its newfound independence through a management buyout, and wasted no time at all in co-founding Third Signal, which is described as a new group of independent studios that'll eventually provide help and resources to other indie teams.

"Some of the best games of the last decade came from teams of 50, not 500. Black Forest Games is one of them, and the right studio to launch Third Signal. Our vision is to build a developer driven group and give teams the independence, resources and creative freedom to continue their creative legacy and bring their own ideas to life," Third Signal CEO Andreas Tobler said in a press release.

Black Forest Games was one of Embracer Group's earliest high-profile acquisitions almost a decade ago, before the company swallowed up countless big names (Lord of the Rings, Tomb Raider, Kingdom Come: Deliverance, more) in the following years and spat back a bunch shortly after. Most infamously, Embracer sold Gearbox and Borderlands during its massive internal restructuring in 2024.

It doesn't sound like Black Forest split with the rights to the Destroy All Humans series or its permanently mean alien protag Crypto, but the studio has said it's still working with THQ Nordic in some capacity. The original Destroy All Humans run nosedived wildly in quality after the second game, so I'm not sure how exciting a remake of, let's say, Destroy All Humans: Big Willy Unleashed would be nowadays, though I'd definitely be interested in seeing Crypto again in another ridiculously silly, sometimes rude and anarchic adventure.

#3706. Publisher Confounds Nintendo By Releasing Two Games With The Same Name At The Same Time On Switch

Earlier this year, Piece by Piece launched on Steam. Then another game, also called Piece by Piece, launched on Steam. Now they’re launching together on the Switch under the same publishing label, because sometimes video games and the people who make them are good.

Despite sharing a name, the two games are vastly different. The Piece by Piece developed by Gamekat and published by No More Robots is a cozy life sim in which a fox tinkerer pieces the broken treasures of his neighbors back together. The other Piece by Piece, developed and published by Neon Polygons, is a game that makes puzzle platforming literal as you piece levels together, jigsaw style. The teams behind the two games became aware of each other after they each announced their release dates.

“Back when we announced the Steam launch date for our Piece by Piece in March, a day later the Piece by Piece from Neon Polygons also announced their launch date, and it was two days after ours,” said Mike Rose, co-founder of No More Robots. He said he got a nervous email from Neon Polygons, concerned that No More Robots would go after them for having a game of the same name. “I got back to them and said ‘Well, that’s just hilarious. Do you wanna bundle up on Steam?'”

In an ecosystem in which developers are desperate for every competitive advantage they can find to stand out amidst the ocean of new games launching daily and devs are taking down demos of their games in fear of AI clones muddying the waters, it’s heartening to see this kind of collaboration. When Rose found out Neon Polygons wanted to port their game to the Switch but couldn’t due to time and financial constraints, he offered to help them out with that too.

“I did it partially because it was a nice / fun thing to do, but I also kinda did it because I love chaos.”

Chaos that continued during the porting process because it turns out Nintendo has a hard time understanding “doing it for the bit.”

“We had to explain over and over again, to each separate Nintendo organization (Europe, Japan, America), that ‘No, sorry but those are two separate games. Yes, they have the same name. Yes, they have the same release date. Yes, we are very sorry. We promise we won’t do this again,'” Rose said.

Piece by Piece and Piece by Piece will launch together on the Switch November 25th.

#3704. Amy Hennig's Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra hasn't been cancelled, Skydance reportedly says, as rumours swirl to the contrary

You'd be forgiven for forgetting that Amy Hennig's superhero game Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra exists, but apparently it's still in development despite its many troubles and rumours to the contrary.

Reassurance comes from Skydance's Slack work chat where, Kotaku says, executive producer Lu Gigliotti told the team they'd spoken "directly" with Skydance leadership and could reassure staff the game wasn't going to be cancelled. "They asked me to make sure you all hear that directly," Gigliotti reportedly told staff. "There is no truth to these claims."

This follows a recent rumour that the action adventure title was potentially going to get the axe in the near future. The rumour originated from a Marvel 1943 fan account, and while the original X post has since been deleted, it didn't stop it from spreading online, including amongst the game's own development staff.

According to Kotaku's report, Rise of Hydra is close to its alpha state, despite seemingly five years of development. The game is said to have had multiple issues through its long development.

The current build is reportedly "light on gameplay", featuring only one interaction button. This is understood to be the result of Rise of Hydra having reportedly been originally envisioned as a Netflix game. According to the same report, the game is late and over budget, which resulted in cuts to its scope and scale throughout development.

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was fully revealed in 2024, and is the debut title of Skydance New Media, the studio headed by veteran designer and writer Amy Hennig, who's famed for her work on the Uncharted series of games.

Though the game was originally planned for release in late 2025, it was later delayed to early 2026 and then again to "beyond early 2026". Earlier this summer, Paramount Games Studio boss Shawn Kittelsen said Rise of Hydra won't be out in 2026, but assured fans it remains in development. According to the report, Rise of Hydra was later delayed to 2027 and beyond.

Tensions are particularly high at the moment following the colossal recent Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, which has already resulted in some job losses at Paramount Games, a group that oversees the game's development, among other projects.

#3703. Kate Middleton, Prince William, King Charles, and Queen Camilla Gather For Remembrance Day

This Sunday, November 8, King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Kate Middleton, Prince William, Princess Anne and other members of the royal family came together to observe Remembrance Sunday, one of the most solemn events on the United Kingdom's calendar. The day marks the anniversary of the armistice that ended World War I, signed on “the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month” in 1918.

The focal point of every Remembrance Day is the Cenotaph in Whitehall, the Portland stone monument where tribute is paid to those who fell in the wars and conflicts in which the country has participated. Every year, representatives of the royal family, political leaders, the Armed Forces, and veterans gather there: This year, more than 10,000 marched alongside the king and the prime minister.

True to tradition, Charles III laid a wreath at the memorial on behalf of the nation and led the royal family. At his side was Prince William, Princess Anne, and the Duke of Edinburgh, who also paid their respects with a floral tribute. Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales, Kate Middleton, watched the ceremony from the balcony of the Foreign Office, as is customary. On the political front, Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath on his first Remembrance Sunday as head of the government, accompanied by Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch and other political leaders.

The day before had already been a day of remembrance: the King, the Queen, and the Princes of Wales attended the Festival of Remembrance at the Royal Albert Hall, the major tribute to the armed forces that precedes Remembrance Sunday.

YES! There are spoilers for You Can See Everything, which is still in theaters as part of the 2026 movie schedule, so proceed accordingly!

One of the tensest scenes in the A24 release that has everyone talking, You Can See Everything, is after the audience gets the surprise appearance from Amanda Seyfried. She and Nathan Fielder make a visit to the home of Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, and their two children. Seyfried had never met Evans or Holmes, despite winning an Emmy for playing the fraudster in The Dropout, which is available with a Hulu subscription.

Seyfried showing up is one of the many WTF moments in the incredible documentary. That wave of disbelief quickly dissipates as she dives headlong into the creative process with co-directors Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, becoming a co-conspirator of sorts. That includes visiting Evans and even talking to Holmes on the phone when she calls from prison.

It’s a scene that had my stomach in knots, and I really wanted to know what was going through Seyfried’s mind. Recently, she finally spoke about the role that she's been keeping quiet about until now. In an interview with Rolling Stone alongside Fielder and Oppenheim and got into what it was like to meet Evans:

It felt dangerous. I wanted answers. We all had this need to understand who was pulling the strings. What he was doing and how he was in the footage that I saw, how you guys were interacting — it felt yucky to me.

Searching for answers is a big reason Seyfried was so into the idea of joining the project when Emma Stone reached out to her about Fielder and the documentary. She wanted answers about Evans, so she became a detective after seeing the footage that had already been filmed. Seyfried explains:

I just wanted any information I could get on Billy. I became this weird Billy detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage. I felt like I needed to meet this guy. It was exciting to me, and it was scary, and it was questionable.

Blurring the lines between reality and surreality is what makes You Can See Everything tick. Seyfried’s willingness, indeed her eagerness, to jump in with both feet is what takes it from a really great documentary to, in my opinion, among the best that’s ever been made.

Eventually, Seyfried would once again play Holmes, recreating scenes with Fielder for his meetings with Holmes in prison that couldn’t be filmed. She got involved without a safety net, and that could lead to an Oscar nomination for the actress. She says she expressed that she was willing to meet Evans, despite the fraught nature of such a meeting, because she felt “protected” by Fielder and Oppenheim, saying:

You wanted that, too, but it had to come from me because I don’t think you would have put me in that position. I did feel protected by you guys pretty early on. I felt like I trusted you.

Trusting Nathan Fielder, as Holmes and Evans found out, isn't always the best course of action, but I'm so glad Seyfried did. The scene at Evans' house is crucial to understanding the whole movie (as best anyone can really understand the motivations of everyone involved). At least we know that Seyfried's intentions were true!

#3699. LACMA Art+Film Gala: Nicole Kidman, Timothée Chalamet Honor Denis Villeneuve

“It’s a pleasure to be here. You guys are just crazy party people,” said artist Vija Celmins as she summed up the jovial atmosphere at the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala during her casual and off-the-cuff acceptance speech as one of the two honorees that night.

The annual fundraiser is a party, and unique among the many galas that hit the town this time of year. Along with raising money for the museum’s initiative to make film more central to its programming (this year it raised a record-breaking almost $7 million), it brings out an eclectic mix of A-list talent, up-and-coming filmmakers, and giants of the art world.

Honoree, Denis Villeneuve, Honoree Vija Celmins, co-chair Eva Chow and LACMA CEO Michael Govan

Just a quick scan of the packed room: Al Pacino sitting with artist Ed Ruscha and art dealer Larry Gagosian; artist Alex Israel wrapping his arm around Orlando Bloom for a photo; model Alex Consani crouching down to chat with influencer and comedian Quenlin Blackwell; and artists Jonas Wood and Mickalene Thomas chatting in one corner while Sarah Paulson and Parker Posey catch up in another.

Anya Taylor-Joy set the mood for the evening as one of the first arrivals on the red carpet, where talent posed in front of Chris Burden’s famed public art installation Urban Light. There in support of Dune director Denis Villeneuve, who was honored along with Celmins, the Dune: Part Two star wore a vintage 1997 Pierre Cardin haute couture bridal gown with a sheer silver overlay that looked both of the past and of the future.

Villeneuve’s leading man, Timothée Chalamet, skipped the carpet altogether, instead slipping into the crowded tent for dinner in a seat next to Villeneuve and his wife, producer Tanya Lapointe. Chalamet arrived separately from girlfriend Kylie Jenner, who did walk the carpet in a low-back Ashi Studio gown. When Jenner arrived at her table, she was seated opposite Chalamet, reaching across to grab his hand.

Seated next to Villeneuve was Nicole Kidman (in a voluminous, ballerina-inspired Chanel dress), who flew 15 hours from Australia to give Villeneuve his award. “The truth is I’ve never really met Denis. I’ve met him on some red carpets and sort of waved at him,” she said during her remarks. “Yet somehow I feel like I know the deepest parts of him because that is what extraordinary filmmakers do. They let you in. They reveal themselves to us through their work. They invite you into their imaginations, into their dreams, into their questions, and into their fears.”

Monica Barbaro, Salma Hayek and Kim Kardashian

Before Villeneuve took the stage, a video capturing his film legacy of big, bold, and personal epics like Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, Arrival, and the Dune trilogy was played, featuring a slew of A-list directors singing his praises, including Steven Spielberg, Alfonso Cuarón, Alejandro González Iñárritu, James Cameron, and Chloé Zhao. “I’ve always felt that cinema is seen as a Pop art—the film carries the burden of being popular in the present,” said Villeneuve in his acceptance speech. “But at the end of the day, the real challenge is to make something that can enter the test of time.”

Speaking of tests (screen tests, that is) Villeneuve got a bit playful with the end of his speech, announcing to the room that he would—right here, right now—announce which actor would play James Bond. The French Canadian director is helming the next Bond film, and over the past week reports have been flying about who might be cast. Would Villeneuve put us all out of our misery and spill the beans? “The actor who will play the next James Bond is—and I will stop right now because [producer] Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack,” he said with a smile.

The gala, once again presented by Gucci, hosted a slew of this Oscar season’s most exciting young filmmakers, including Obsession filmmaker Curry Barker and Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman, along with La Bola Negra directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known as Los Javis). The latter told me they didn’t plan to party as hard as they did at the Academy Museum Gala a few weeks ago, where they went viral for singing along to Taylor Swift’s performance of “Love Story.” Said Ambrossi, “I’m drinking only water tonight.”

Among the other guests at the gala (which had additional support by Audi), Joel Edgerton chatted with Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson and Daniel Scheinert, one half of the Oscar-winning directing team Daniels (Everything Everywhere All at Once). Kim Kardashian wove her way through the crowd, pausing perfectly to look over her shoulder for a trailing photographer. And several stars made a date night out of the event: Sienna Miller brought fiancé Oli Green; Julia Garner sat with musician Charlie Walker; Viola Davis enjoyed the night with husband and producing partner Julius Tennon. Paris Hilton, who introduced Rosé onstage with her classic catchphrase “that’s hot,” wore a glittering Jenny Packham gown as she cascaded through the room with her husband, Carter Reum.

Eva Chow, who had co-chaired the gala for the past 15 years with Leonardo DiCaprio, announced that she’d be stepping down from her post after this year. Dubbed the “Culture Queen of Los Angeles,” she is credited with bringing together Hollywood and the art world for the event, helping grow it into the must-attend party of the season. DiCaprio couldn’t make it this year because he has a cold, but his girlfriend, model Vittoria Ceretti, was there to represent him.

But with all these big Hollywood types in the room, it was Celmins who stole the show—though she didn’t mean to. In a video that ran before her acceptance speech, the artist welcomed the video crew into her home, revealing her quick-witted humor, her ornery cat (she claims to be a dog person), and her love of Bob Dylan. Celmins is best known for her boundless work inspired by nature, including ocean waves, desert floors, and starry night skies. She charmed the crowd with her boundless personality as well.

LACMA had plenty to celebrate this year too. After a 20-year-long planning and development process, the David Geffen Galleries were completed this past year. As partygoers entered the tent for dinner, the silhouette of the formidable new building stood out in the background. “Same tent. Different buildings around it,” joked LACMA CEO Michael Govan during his opening remarks.

After his speech, Villeneuve and all the guests made their way out to LACMA’s main courtyard, where Rosé would perform under the stars. I joked with him that I thought he would make some news with that tease of a Bond casting, and then wondered if he likes being the center of attention at a gala like this. He said he values the connections he makes with other filmmakers and artists at these events. “I like talking one-on-one,” he said.

Noor Alfallah, Al Pacino, Erica Pelosini, Larry Gagosian and Ed Ruscha

While Rosé performed four songs for the black-tie-clad audience, Emily in Paris star Ashley Park and In the Heights actor Anthony Ramos swayed to her ballad “Number One Girl.” Popcorn and cotton candy were passed out to the audience, which, naturally, sang along when Rosé ended her set with her biggest hit, “APT.” Andrew Garfield led his Artificial costar Monica Barbaro by the hand through the crowd. Though the pair didn’t pose for photos on the carpet together, the couple (who have been romantically linked since 2025) spent the evening in close contact as they chatted with friends like Salma Hayek Pinault.

Villeneuve’s speech best captured the evening’s one-of-a-kind mash-up of art and film when he spoke passionately about the importance of human effort in the era of AI. “I can create something with a prompt, or I can go into the desert with actors, with a crew, and go on a real adventure where I learn about life and become better at my craft,” he said. “More important than the result is the process. The process is how the human experience acquires its meaning. In this moment in time, it is more important than ever that human beings keep making art together.”

Odessa A'zion in a Charles & Ron + Maison Privee coat.

#3698. Will a Grand Theft Auto game ever be set outside of America? Rockstar offers a small glimmer of hope

The Grand Theft Auto games have always been synonymous with America; Americana is baked into the crime series' very being. Across its history, there's only ever been one GTA game set outside America: the London-based expansion of the original game.

GTA 6 follows this template, parodying the American state of Florida and the city of Miami. But what about the next game - will the series always be in America? Not necessarily.

In an interview with The Guardian, Rockstar North co-studio boss Rob Nelson propped the proverbial door open a sliver by saying: "Never say never." He then quickly followed that comment with: "But there’s still so much to do in America".

This is a topic Rockstar has responded to before, most notably when company co-founder and long-time GTA writer Dan Houser - who's no longer at Rockstar - discussed why the series always seemed to return to America. He said it was because cities like Miami and New York and Los Angeles are places where extreme juxtapositions exist. They're places where extreme wealth rubs shoulders with extreme poverty, and where organised crime can be found.

There's also something America infamously has that few other countries do, and that's free availability of guns, which is such a core tenet of a GTA experience.

Nevertheless, Obbe Vermeij - a former technical director at Rockstar North - revealed last year that a GTA: Tokyo almost happened. However, it wasn't going to be made by Rockstar but rather an external team in Japan.

While discussing the subject, Vermeij referred to America as "basically the epicenter of Western culture". "Everybody knows the cities, even people who haven't been there," Vermeij said. "They have a mental image of the cities. I'm afraid we're stuck in this loop of about five American cities. Let's just get used to it."

GTA 6 is just days away from its 19th November release on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. Rockstar recently clarified the game runs at 30FPS across all platforms and confirmed that while it's available through Xbox Cloud Gaming, it cannot be streamed to PCs or non-Xbox devices.

#3697. Grand Theft Auto 5: The Kotaku Re-Review

Grand Theft Auto V is the reigning game of all time. One of gamingâs most undeniable cultural exports. An ugly game that casts one unbelievable shadow. A title so massive, itâs become damn near impossible to recreate without burning down your development studio in 2026. Revisiting it in the lead-up to GTA VIâs release later this year has been illuminating in many ways, but the thing Iâm perhaps most struck by about the 2013 hit is how miserable it is. What a fascinating thing to exist in the supposed upper echelon of the gaming pantheon.

GTA V is filled with all kinds of missions and objectivesâthe stuff that modern gaming parlance constantly calls “content.” Really, it turns everything into content for you to check off. It’s got big missions and small ones. Simple, boring ones that occasionally lull you to sleep. Distractions like tennis and drag racing. And, on the other end, massive, multi-part setpieces that get the blood pumping a little more efficiently. A gulf separates these sequences. Sometimes I’m little more than a glorified cabbie, at other times a glorified avatar of the âAmerican dreamââa ball of boredom, rage, and discontent at The Way Things Are, armed with a rifle aimed at nothing in particular.

Lots of it feels utterly meaningless. Stealing the occasional getaway vehicle and quietly parking it in a nearby lot often counts as a mission, one I hate after doing it multiple times in my ~50 hours revisiting GTA V. Not that its more pulse-pounding action is especially noteworthy either. The game’s crosshair, for example, is wholly unremarkable. It’s just a dot. A dot that, by default, magnetizes to the often nameless nobodies on the other end of your barrel, as if to smooth any friction that could possibly arise in the instant between when you see a foe and when you pull the trigger on your weapon of choice.Â

Many other shooters feature different crosshairs depending on the weapon. A grenade launcher might suggest an arc. A sniper rifle, too. A shotgun blast has a wider spread, and a crosshair usually indicates its range. But time and time again, GTA V plays it cool, calm, and detached with its minimalist crosshair. It doesn’t want to bore you with calculating distances and trajectories. It wants you to endlessly put holes in cops, gangsters, hillbillies, rival drug enterprises, federal agents, clowns, aliens, and everything in between, while occasionally piloting several classes of vehicle in increasingly linear scenarios. It doesn’t feel wholly good or bad; it feels likeâ¦nothing.Â

Driving around the state of San Andreas and shooting things feels like nothing. A kind of nothing that quicklyâeasilyâfills dozens of hours. Like a chore. Maybe that’s the best way to describe GTA V. Well, if itâs going to be such a chore, it feels, at least, like GTA V should aim that tedium at some larger point, shouldn’t it?

It kind of does. Each of its endeavors, be it a mundane task, an odd job to rustle up some cash, or a riotous heist spilled out on the streets of not-LA, does in fact feel pointed. Compulsive, even. At least in part because they feel like the backdrop for the gameâs occasionally devastating musings that hit with the force of, well, a getaway vehicle.Â

The most consequential series of missions among GTA V‘s errands is largely divorced from the thrust of its campaign. Itâs got nothing to do with heists and has nothing to do with two-thirds of the gameâs playable trio. Itâs got nothing to do with the city of Los Santos, even. Far up in the middle of Nowhere, Blaine County, is an unsavory duo called the Minute Men, who are on a collision course with a similarly ugly force by the name of Trevor Phillipsâa walking, talking (usually swearing) cancer and truly one of the most detestable protagonists a game has ever saddled a player with.Â

The Minute Menâs contributions to GTA V are small but important. Over a triptych of morally repugnant descents into darkness that only Trevor can take on, they try to prove the righteousness of their cause. In a move that felt like a cavity opening in my soul, Trevor rides along with Joe and Josef, two members of the âCivil Border Patrol,â as they chase down and detain Mexican-American citizens across the countryside. Or as one of them says, in his native Russian on American soil, âWell-motivated people, eager to do low-level jobs at any wage to support their families.âÂ

These missions are, like the rest of GTA Vâs offerings, pretty unremarkable in their construction. You chase after these poor souls in a patrol vehicleâa park rangerâs van with hardly a new splash of paintâtase them (another drab crosshair) and eventually escort them back to the vehicle, where they are subsequently driven to a somewhat ambiguous fate. The whole thing would only run about 15 minutes if the missions were stitched together, and ends with little fanfare.

All in all, these excursions with the Civil Border Patrol are a perfect microcosm of what GTA V actually excels at: being a banal cascade of senseless violence and bigotry, bookended by a smug but empty wink. A shockingly vivid reflection of our depravity and our inability to break from it. A post-modern vision of what passes for a video game and what can be fun about it.Â

Many of GTA Vâs most memorable moments echo this particular sensibility, as has become customary of the franchise, which has satirized America and its long-running series of systemic failures over the past 25 years. The mission “Friend Request,” which involves another of the gameâs protagonists, named Michael, breaking into the headquarters of a Facebook analog called Life Invader, is a perfect example. In it Michael, and thus the player, live out what has become, in the years since the gameâs release, an even more entertaining fantasy, making a very public example of a tech mogul with an inflated ego and a penchant for flagrant violations of child labor laws. A real crowd pleaser, that one.Â

But even this fantasy is relatively dry. Breaking in consists of buying some clothes and walking up to the building. At that point, you sit through cutscenes and eventually substitute a prototype device with a bomb for the one meant to be used in the big presentation. Then, once Michael is miles away and watching the mogulâs press conference on his living room TV, you can call the deviceâs number, triggering the bomb and blowing his head off. A novelty to be sure in 2013, but one that barely masks GTA V‘s boorishness in 2026.

For every win like the Life Invader sequence, there is another return to GTA Vâs morose throughline. A throughline which brings you to a mission where you must profile a party through a sniper scope and take out a target at the behest of shady government boys. In the same breath, another of your characters is recreating Gitmo in an unmarked warehouse elsewhere in GTA Vâs beautifully rendered facsimile of sunny California and torturing an innocent man. Almost as if looking at the camera and saying, âOf course it happens here.â

I can still feel the haptics of my Dualsense simulating my victimâs palpitations throughout the extended playable sequence, the uncomfortable sensation of feeling like I held his heart in my hands as the game compelled me to waterboard him and smash his limbs with the biggest wrench youâve ever seen.Â

At the missionâs end, Trevor whisks his barely-there prisoner away and, rather than executing him, lets him go. He only does this, however, after berating his victim all the way to the airport and unpacking his own thoughts about the effectiveness of torture, at one point shouting, “The media and the government would have us believe that torture is some necessary thing. We need it to get information, to assert ourselves.” Trevor, who’s just spent the last hour or so maiming this poor soul, reveals that he sees through the lie that America has propped up about torture. What a hypocrite!

He not only recognizes the facade, he explicitly acknowledges that all the violence he just inflicted on the man in his passenger seatâa man who, a short time earlier, heâd tortured with enough electricity to briefly stop his heartâwas for naught. Or rather, it wasn’t for the sake of actually gathering information, since none was actually gained from the act. No, it was instead a pretense for Trevor and his FIB handler to get their jollies off by bringing a guy uncomfortably close to death.Â

And so Trevor concludes, “Torture’s for the torturer. Or the guy giving the orders to the torturer.” He claims that the only way for his victim to move forward in lifeâto not get further rolled by America, the government, the world, and men like Trevorâis clearly to abandon his family and morals and become a torture advocate rather than a protestor in light of this experience. To join the side that just did him material harm to not risk further ire. To prop up a lie and man’s capacity for cruelty rather than try to make the world a meaningfully better place. To roll around in the shit with the rest of the pigs.

Though GTA V was first released in the fall of 2013, this whole scene is a grim punchline that smacks of truths yet to come. Look at the world of difference between Kyle Rittenhouse and David Hogg: two young white men whose futures were unquestionably molded by gun violenceâanother of this countryâs failuresâand whose trajectories could not be more different. An advocate and a protestor.

The former shot three men, killing two, amidst protests of police and gun violence. In return, he was valorized by right-wing media and segments of America, even meeting the then-sitting president and being acquitted of any wrongdoing. He started up a short-lived YouTube channel where he espoused pro-gun rhetoric, but after being cleared of all charges, he eventually settled back into life as a private citizen. As if he didn’t travel across state lines with a weapon and LARP as a cop as a 17-year-old boy. As if he didnât kill people.

Nowadays, Rittenhouse and his wife live in Sarasota, where it was recently discovered that he works in a shop doing what he loves: selling and talking about guns. He might even play a bunch of GTA V for all I know. Hell, he probably canât wait for its quickly approaching sequel this November.

The latter survived a school shooting as a young man, became an anti-gun advocate in the wake of his personal tragedy, and has often been met with derision and skepticism as heâs attempted to climb the political ladder and reform gun policies in the U.S. His election to vice chair of the Democratic National Committee ended in an ousting once it was apparent that his progressive politics threatened establishment Dems.Â

Though Hogg made inroads over the yearsâeven being paraded by the political left in the way the right did with Rittenhouseâ his attempts to prevent another shooting like the one that set him on this path have constantly been stymied. By who? A governing body and segment of the populace that would rather fight for the right to arm themselves and shoot up another school, or arm a kid and set him loose amid a riot, than protect its children and most vulnerable communities.Â

Who does it sound like made out alright in the end? And with that said, can we really say that Trevor, and GTA V as a whole, is that full of shit?

It’s kind of remarkable how many shots GTA V calls throughout its campaign, how many clear displays of our moral decay were so apparent when this game was released in 2013. How clearly Rockstar saw where things were headed. Later in the game, once Michael takes a job working on a movie, heâs confronted with a problem: A producer on his high-budget, and by all accounts good, movie would rather can the basically finished product and claim the insurance than release it into the world. What extinction-level crisis that has rocked the entertainment industry for the last several years does that sound like?

This prescience makes GTA V a stunning thing to behold at least for its ability to recognize that weâve always had this kind of capacity for cruelty, both overt and mundane. Whether itâs a barbarous radio ad playing in the background of a scenic drive up to the countryside, or the way that countless white men in GTA V default to calling the sole Black protagonist âhomie,â GTA V nails the casualization of our worst base instincts and how it has seemingly bled into every fiber of our being in a late-stage capitalist nightmare and the decline of an empire.

Itâs compelling how miserable GTA V is, especially in light of the fantasy the game is trying to sell players. The sunny âhavenâ of 2010s liberalism that is Los Santos. The promise of upwards mobility, no matter how desperate the measures that the crew takes. Try hard (and rob some banks) and you too can perhaps shoot your way out of every one of your problems. Be bad, be so bad that you somehow work your way back to being good.Â

This extends to GTA Online as well: a playground for the rich to torture the average person with lavish displays of wealth and power. A setting where it can be damn near impossible to take in the sights and sounds of the city without getting mowed down by your fellow man in an armored car with mounted guns or a flying bike. A place where everyone else is banging down your door and hitting your line to make money because money is the only fuel for a life worth living.

And while Iâd love to assume many of its players âworked hardâ to get where they are over the years, GTA Onlineâs chart-topping microtransactions for the last decade, which have turned the multiplayer suite into a veritable cash cow for Rockstar Games, indicate to me that quite a lot of people were, in fact, fine with taking a shortcut or two to the top, and subsequently made it everyone elseâs problem.Â

Itâs a toxic game down to the marrow, and goddamn does that make it much more interesting a text and much richer a place to walk around in. Especially because it does just look and sound like our reality, our lived experiences, our cities, our prejudices, and our cultures.

We live in a perpetual state of sharp contrasts. Whether it’s a picturesque train ride upstate, an exceptionally designed building, the beautiful art spray-painted on its side, or a random act of kindness observed in the street, we all see beautiful signs of life everywhere we go. And at the same time that those things are true, there have seemingly never been more pointless wars, more humanitarian crises abroad and at home, and more negligence and abject cruelty on the part of our worldâs power-hungry leaders. Even video games, a reprieve from many of these woes for many, canât fully separate themselves from the conditions that brought them into being. How do you untangle one from the other? How do you fix that? Can you? Or can you just sit back and laugh at it?

Perhaps the most miserable thing about GTA V is that it canât really imagine a way out, just a constant state of being. There is no up for Michael, who dreams of a life like the movies and largely settles for a life with his dysfunctional family instead. Nor is there anything better down the line for the mentally ill and unstable Trevor Phillips or for Franklin, who often feels tokenized by the game and simply caught in the gravitational pull of the former two and their age-old grudge match. There is only a status quo to maintain.Â

There is no vision of a Los Santos, or a U.S. for that matter, after GTA V that recovers from its many ills. Just as there is probably no version of the series that ever stops reflecting the countryâs worst, and perhaps most obvious, tendencies. I struggle to call this unremarkable, like I would its gameplay, or truly unimaginative. Poignant, perhaps. Miserable, yeah. Tragic, for sure.

And for that, and so much more, GTA V is still the reigning game of all time. At least until the next one.Â

Guangyun Chen promises an "optimised client" to reduce stuttering and performance issues.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Recently, there's been some debate in the community regarding the use of mods and configs. Our stance is clear: Marvel Rivals is a fair competitive game. Any use of mods or configs to get an unfair combat advantage is unacceptable, and we will take action against it. This is our bottom line.

"These forbidden modifications include altering maps into minimalist 'potato' models, amplifying footstep audio, removing screen shake, and so on. Furthermore, some of these modifications employ memory injection. Since this behaviour is functionally identical to using cheats, we will handle them accordingly." via a dev diary.

How far would you go to achieve decent frame rates? Well some Marvel Rivals players have been breaking the rules to try and give themselves a better shot of having a sort of salvageable in-game experience.

Sure, a lot of players using mods and configs are doing so to give themselves the "unfair combat advantage" that Guangyun Chen talks about, using it to dial down the map detail so enemy players stand out more or heightening environmental tells like footsteps. But that doesn't account for absolutely everyone within the community, with some changing their configs to try and remove the stuttering that can plague Marvel Rivals games.

Marvel Rivals has always had an issue with its performance. I shrugged it off as teething pain at first but it's been almost two years since release, and not much has changed. Five months ago NetEase released an "experimental feature" to try and dial down the game's insatiable appetite for RAM, and while it reduced the frequency of game crashes, it didn't solve stuttering.

Then the decision was then made in July to enact some changes that could help with the visual clutter players experience during games. It was brought on by the addition of Jubilee, who had particularly messy VFX. I didn't notice much of a change; team fights are still as chaotic, messy, and confusing as ever.

The biggest change for good happened a few months ago when Marvel Rivals managed to shave an impressive 40GB off by completely repackaging its assets. But by and large things haven't improved fast enough, and Guangyun Chen even accepts that players messing with configs for better performance do have a valid point.

"We also recognise that a core desire behind players using mods or tweaking configs is simply wanting better framerates and a cleaner visual environment," Guangyun Chen adds. "We are actively working on this. In season 11, thanks to the hard work of our programming team, we'll be rolling out an optional, experimental optimised client.

"This optimisation targets the logic load on the CPU during matches. When toggled on, it will provide up to a 10% boost in CPU performance and significantly reduce mid-combat stuttering. You can download the corresponding DLC on PC and then enable this experimental feature directly in the game launcher."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The Marvel Rivals team is also testing a "clearer competitive" VFX setting which sounds like it will essentially do what some are accomplishing with mods and configs right now: "tweaking the visual effects" for every hero to make fights more legible for players. I am, however, not yet convinced. I've been waiting for huge improvements in Marvel Rivals for so long now that I'll only believe it when I see it.

#3695. Paradox boss Frederik Wester stepping down after several tumultuous years for the Cities Skylines and Stellaris publisher

Deputy CEO Mattias Lilja taking over role.

Paradox Interactive's Frederik Wester has announced he's stepping down from the role of CEO after a combined decade and a half leading the company. The news follows several tumultuous years for the publisher best known for grand strategy games including Stellaris, Europa Universalis, and Crusader Kings 3.

In a statement announcing the change in leadership, Paradox said Wester had "decided to step down as CEO to continue focusing on the company's long-term development as a member of the Board." Paradox's current deputy CEO, Mattias Lilja, will take over Wester's role from 4th January 2027. Wester is to remain in the position until then in order "to ensure an orderly transition".

"I'm truly grateful to all our engaged players and talented colleagues who contribute to outstanding gaming experiences every day," Wester said of his decision. "They are the ones who made these years amazing. My plan was never to be CEO for life. The goal was to build the foundation before passing the baton on for the next chapter in the company's journey. Since I returned as CEO, we've streamlined our strategy, rebuilt our pipeline and developed our commercial offering. Mattias has had a central role in laying this foundation, and now is the right time to hand over. Given his experience and vision, he is exceptionally well positioned to take the company to its next level."

Wester has twice served as Paradox CEO since joining the company in 2003. His first stint ran from 2009 to 2018, after which he became Paradox's executive chairman of the board. He returned to the CEO role in 2021, and has overseen a troubled period for the company. This has included the embattled development of Vampire: The Masquerade Bloodlines 2 - which finally launched last October after multiple delays, near cancellation, and a switch in developer. Unfortunately the game failed to resonate with critics and audiences, and Paradox announced a 162 percent decline in operating profit earlier this year as a result of its commercial failure.

Wester's most recent watch - which began with an admittance of "inappropriate behaviour" amid a damning report into Paradox's workplace culture - has also seen the high-profile cancellation of Sims competitor Life By You, an indefinite delay for Prison Architect 2 after Paradox parted ways with original developer Double Eleven, and a split with BattleTech studio Harebrained Schemes following the commercial failure of The Lamplighters League. Paradox's Cities Skylines 2 has also been blighted with controversy: after a disastrous launch in 2023, its console release is still yet to emerge, and development is now being handled by a new studio after Paradox split with former developer Colossal Order last year. In 2004, Wester admitted the publisher had "made the wrong calls in several projects".

Despite all this, incoming CEO Mattias Lilja remains buoyant. "Paradox has a unique DNA that has made us one of the greats in deep and engaging strategy and management games," he wrote in a statement announcing his promotion. "Now we’re stepping up the pace: we will make further investments in our core business, push the boundaries of our game design, work even more closely with our loyal players, develop more and better tools and services that benefit both modders and players, and continue to sharpen our ways of working and our organisation, with player value in focus."

Paradox, does of course, have some promising games on its upcoming slate. Alongside continued work on grand strategy stalwarts like Crusader Kings 3, Europa Universalis 5, and Stellaris, next year sees the release of Lego Skylines, and post-apocalyptic grand strategy game Afterworld is also on the way.

When Eiji Aonuma showed off gameplay for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake back in September, one of the features he highlighted was Link’s new ability to sprint, saying it had been added explicitly after he observed players spamming Link’s dodge-roll ability to move faster in the original.

But unfortunately for Aonuma, the verdict is in: rolling is still faster, even than Link’s new sprint.

In the original game, Link ran at a single speed, with Epona serving to speed him up in the later game. However, speedrunners and even regular players would frequently spam Link’s dodge-roll ability to move faster before Epona was available, because rolling constantly was faster than just walking.

This dodge-roll spamming has apparently been on Aonuma’s mind ever since, because while showing off the sprint in the gameplay demonstration, he said, “In the original game, I believe some players rolled to get around faster. Now, if you hold down the A button, you roll, then dash like this. Dashing is recommended whenever you’re traveling longer distances.”

However, speedrunners of the remake have already timed everything out, and rolling is…still faster.

Aonuma didn’t explicitly say that the rolling bothered him, but it’s funny that he called it out in the presentation. His citing of this specific player behavior suggests that he’s had this on his mind for years as something he wanted to change, right up there with his statement that fixing the Water Temple was “overdue homework.”

I do think Aonuma has likely succeeded with his sprint even so, as it’s notÂ much slower than the rollâcertainly there’s not the same gulf between it and the roll as there once was between Link’s regular speed and the roll. Most normal players will probably embrace the sprint this time around. Speedrunners, well, I expect they’ll be doing far weirder things than rolling.

Oh, wait, they already are. It turns out that doing a front hop andÂ then a roll isÂ even faster. Sorry, Aonuma!

#3692. After two weeks of multiplayer downtime, Dark Souls 2 & 3's mysterious server "issue" has been fixed, so it no longer feels so lonely online

Developer FromSoftware has announced that online multiplayer servers for Dark Souls 2 and 3 are back online following a nearly two-week outage.

FromSoftware temporarily disabled multiplayer on 30th October, citing what it called "a server issue". Some speculated this could be related to the recently discovered PHP security bug, which impacted a number of other games.

FromSoftware never specified the exact issue impacting its servers, and today's statement is equally vague. "Regarding the temporary suspension of the game server for Dark Souls 2, and Dark Souls 3, the investigation has been completed and the fix has been applied. The game server and online features are now restored," a notice on Dark Souls' official site reads.

"We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience caused, and thank you for your patience and understanding."

Online servers do more in FromSoftware games than simply facilitating co-op and PvP; they're also responsible for handling messages players leave for each other in-game, as well as the ghostly representations of players who just went through the same area, helping the Dark Souls series' forlorn worlds feel a little less solitary.

This isn't the first time Dark Souls servers have gone offline, either. In 2022, servers for all three games went offline due to a vulnerability that allowed malicious code to run on them. In that instance, it took FromSoftware three months to bring servers back online for some games, and as many as nine months for others.

In other FromSoftware news, the studio recently announced - following months of speculation - it's officially delaying the Switch 2-exclusive The Duskbloods to sometime in 2027.

#3690. The Witcher 3 uses gen-AI to enhance Geralt's Polish voice following actor's stroke - "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically"

"I have great trust ... for the creators of this game."

CD Projekt Red has revealed that it used - and is using - generative AI technology to treat and alter the voice of the Polish actor who portrayed Geralt of Rivia in upcoming Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past.

The actor, Jacek Rozenek, has portrayed Geralt of Rivia in all the major Witcher games, meaning his voice has become as synonymous with the role in Poland as Doug Cockle's has for people playing in English. But Rozenek suffered a severe stroke in 2019 that left him temporarily unable to speak, and when he was able to talk and perform again, the tonality and quality of his voice had changed.

It's for these reasons that CD Projekt Red - with Rozenek's consent - employed the help of a company called Respeecher to alter the lines he recorded for The Witcher 3's Songs of the Past expansion using generative-AI technology. As confirmed to Game File, an AI trained on Rozenek's previous Witcher work is retreating his recordings to make them sound more like the Geralt you hear elsewhere in The Witcher 3.

"The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," Jacek Rozenek explained. "I have great trust ... for the creators of this game."

Game File heard both treated and untreated recordings of Rozenek's Songs of the Past work, and reported a "significant" difference between them. Rozenek's untreated voice was apparently "deep and gravelly" and "noticeably rougher than his recordings for the original game". But treated, the voice was "far smoother and sounds younger", and closer to the original Witcher 3 Geralt recordings.

This isn't the first time CD Projekt Red has used generative AI for voice recordings in one of its games. The studio worked with Respeecher in 2023 to produce new voiceover lines for Cyberpunk 2077 expansion Phantom Liberty. Viktor Vektor actor Miłogost "Miłek" Reczek passed away in 2021, after the original game was released, and CD Projekt Red didn't want to recast the role. Reczek's sons apparently gave their blessing for their father's voice to be artificially generated.

"I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically with consent and also to do something good," CD Projekt Red localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed told Game File, referring to the Rozenek recordings.

"For future projects, when we consider Geralt is becoming older and has a deeper voice, this is not a problem for us at all. It's more about this specific situation here, where we have both the voice from 12 years ago and from now next to each other, which could kind of take people out of the experience and feel that there is this difference."

The third Witcher 3 expansion, Songs of the Past, releases at some point next year, an unprecedented 12 years after the original game launched. It adds an entirely new region, Letten, and centres its main story around Geralt's missing bardic bestie Dandelion, whose family lives there.

In preparation for the expansion, a remastered version of The Witcher 3 was released a couple of months ago, overhauling the old role-playing adventure and bringing its baseline presentation more in line with what we'd expect from a modern game; it also overhauled some animations and enemy behaviours and reworked skill trees. For that reason, old-gen consoles PS4 and Xbox One won't receive the Songs of the Past expansion, despite The Witcher 3 being available on them.

#3688. Benito Skinner’s ‘Overcompensating’ Returns for Season 2: More Laughs, More Sex, More Gay

It’s been a year and a half since the first season of Benito Skinner’s Prime Video comedy series, Overcompensating, debuted, and a lot has changed for him in that time. For one, Skinner—also known as Benny Drama, his online alter ego—is blond now. It’s a change he says may be permanent or perhaps semipermanent. “It’s how I see myself—as a blond,” he tells me over Zoom. “So we’re going to keep going with it for a sec.”

But Skinner has transformed in much less superficial ways since the launch of his hit Amazon series, which is based on his experiences coming out as gay as a Georgetown undergrad. Equal parts raunchy and heartwarming, the first season follows Benny (Skinner), a closeted former high school football player who attempts to navigate the chaos of college, where he forms an unlikely bond with a fellow student named Carmen (Wally Baram).

Skinner shares that making the second installment of the series was “way more fluid, way less stressed.” As it should have been. The first season was a popular hit for the streamer (it has a 93% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes), hard-launching Skinner as an exciting new voice plucked from the internet and ready for prime time.

Benny and Carmen begin the season as enemies.

The second season, which Vanity Fair can exclusively reveal will debut on February 17, 2027, expands the world he created with new storylines for the supporting characters—and bigger stakes for Benny as he comes into his own with his sexuality. Benny navigates not only coming out to his sister, Grace (Mary Beth Barone), and his parents (Connie Britton and Kyle MacLachlan), but also his own sexual exploration—and all the awkwardness that comes with it.

So much of what made the first season a hit—the awkward comedy, the silly themed parties, the talking Megan Fox poster—returns, but this time many of the characters grapple with deeper issues. Yet Skinner felt lighter making the show this time around. “I think in season one, Benny is that stressed, so that kind of worked,” he says. “But in this one, we’re having more fun. He has some joy, so we can loosen up a little bit.”

Connie Britton, center, reprises her role as Benny's mom.

After Overcompensating premiered, Skinner was approached, he says, by “a few gays” who told him, “I thought it’d be gayer, the show.” He promises that the second season delivers just that: “We’re creeping out of the closet,” says Skinner.

In the first season, Benny is trying to find his place on campus while constantly living in fear that the people around him will discover he’s gay. He falls for a dashing British classmate named Miles (Rish Shah), only to find out he is straight and has kissed Carmen. The season ends with Carmen revealing that she has also slept with Grace’s boyfriend, Peter (Adam DiMarco), and in the final moments, Carmen accidentally lets slip in front of Grace that Benny is gay.

Skinner and Lukas Gage reunite in season two.

In the upcoming season, Benny heads back home with his sister for the start of Christmas break, struggling because he hasn’t yet come out to his family. “If season one was about friends, I think this season is about family, and trying to reintroduce yourself to your parents after starting to become yourself,” says Skinner. The way his father finds out about it makes for an especially tense moment, and Benny goes to great lengths (like joining the crew team) to mend that bond with his dad. “That relationship between gay men and father, I think, is always fraught and confusing,” he says. “I just wanted to make it as honest as possible.”

At the start of the new season, Benny and Carmen are at odds; Grace and her boyfriend, Peter, have broken up; and many of the characters are exploring those feelings of loneliness that can crop up in college. A handful of exciting new faces also join this season. Australian actor Aisha Dee (The Bold Type) plays a new student who becomes an instant It girl on campus. AnnaSophia Robb (The Carrie Diaries) joins as an intense coxswain (the one who does the yelling) on the crew team. And Tony-nominated stage actor Tom Francis (Sunset Boulevard) plays the captain of the team, serving as Benny’s newest love interest.

Peter (Adam DiMarco) is looking for his path forward.

For Skinner, the second season is about capturing the ups and downs of coming out. It’s not just one reveal and then you’re out of the closet and everything is better. “I get to be even more specific about coming out and also tell a story that I think I haven’t seen yet done in this way, which is the complication of coming out—how you can take 10 steps forward, a hundred steps back,” he says.

Benny joins the crew team, where he meets a new love interest (Tom Francis).

There’s also a lot more sex. “There are a couple scenes that are definitely going to be off-limits for the family,” Skinner says. But of course, in Overcompensating, the sex scenes aren’t always smooth sailing. “I think our show is about trying to be sexy and then it going wrong, or feeling like you start to come into yourself but you get made a fool,” he says.

Skinner adds the title of executive music producer to his résumé this season. “It feels like a return to my radio-DJ roots, and that feels right,” he says. There’s more Britney Spears and Charli xcx (who appeared in a cameo last season), and he wanted the show’s music to remain an important part of the world. He even wrote a letter to Coldplay when he wanted to use the band’s song “Fix You” in this new season. “I love doing the letters to these guys because I’m like, So is Chris Martin reading this? Is this sent by owl? What’s the vibe?” he says with a smile.

Overcompensating’s return will come almost two years after its debut, and Skinner, who says he always plans to keep this story set in the characters’ college years, wants to make the wait a little shorter next time. “I apologize to everyone that it took a while,” he says. “TV takes a long time, so I’m trying to go faster, but daddy has to write it.”

“I don’t want any of these characters to feel like we’re pandering to maybe what we think the internet will want,” says Skinner of crafting the second installment after a hit first season.

“What I wanted to do is surprise people with where we took it,” says Skinner of the new season, “and have them be like, ‘Oh, this isn’t what I asked for, but it is something kind of delicious and new.’”

Jensen Huang has resigned from his role as CEO and president of Nvidia. He will be replaced by interim CEO, Colette Kress, who had previously worked as the company's CFO for a long stretch.

"Nvidia Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately," a statement on Nvidia's newsroom says.

Jensen Huang has been embroiled in a scandal, or rather a couple of scandals, over the past few weeks.

First, an affair to which he later admitted; suggested to have been with a datacentre company executive suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.

Second, another alleged affair, this time with an executive at Nvidia.

The markets may get spooked by the announcement, as Huang was a co-founder of the business (founded in 1993, making Huang the longest CEO of a major tech firm) and has overseen the company through its latest and largest success.

The share price for the company had already plummeted to its lowest levels since June 2025 following a report that the company's board was considering ousting Huang.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

The company's share price is currently down around 12% in pre-market trading.

The move to appoint the company's long-standing CFO as interim CEO was an expected one, to help ease the transition from Huang's leadership. Intel did something similar when the company ousted its CEO in 2018.

"Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Nvidia, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates."

Huang has also resigned from his position as president and from his board seat, which may ease some concerns in recent days that his significant stake and power in the company would be tough to expunge should the company board try to push him out.

Now, the job for the remaining Nvidia employees is to find the next full-time CEO. That could take some time.

The actor recorded over 10,000 lines for the original game, work that Respeecher used in creating its algorithm for his voice. âGetting there took dozens of hours, training models, going through the details with the CDPR team, and dealing with AI artifacts that never fully disappear,â Dmytro Vasylets, a synthetic speech artist for the company, told Game File. âThe hardest part was Jacekâs emotional range: the half-tones, shouts, groans, anger, fear and laughter. Capturing all of that at the highest audio quality was the real challenge. Iâd like to think we pulled it off.â

CDPR said it wasn’t planning to use the algorithm to alter Rozenek’s voice in the future, suggesting that his now lower, gruffier voice would be fine for the appearance of an older, gruffier Geralt in a game like The Witcher 4. The voice actor, meanwhile, confirmed he has not listened to his AI doppelganger and it doesn’t sound like he’s planning to anytime soon.

#3685. I'm Not Against Fairy Smut, But I Still Reject That Label For ACOTAR

The romantasy series is so much more than just that.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

First and foremost, I have nothing against smut, fairy or otherwise, so this is by no means a judgment on the term frequently used (often by its own fans) to describe extra spicy romance and romantasy books. We like what we like, and sometimes that includes a lil spice. Or a lot, whatever. That being said, I'm also in agreement with the fans of Sarah J. Maas' ACOTAR and other romantasy series who oppose these books being reduced to the label of "fairy smut," especially if it's to explain why they're so popular. While some romantic fantasy books may be adored primarily for how sexually graphic they are, I just don't believe that's the case for ACOTAR.

Having devoured A Court of Splintered Harmony, the sixth book in Sarah J. Maas' A Court of Thorns and Roses (aka ACOTAR) series, much quicker than I wish I had when it arrived in October, my Instagram feed is now chock full of reactions to the novel, memes and theories. The discourse should hopefully sustain me for weeks, while I wait alongside other ACOTAR fans for Book 7, A Court of Forgotten Melody, to hit shelves in January. Among the topics that came across my feed recently were reactions (often frustrated ones) to the use of the term "fairy smut" to describe the ACOTAR books.

The New York Times used the term 'fairy smut' – or, more specifically, it refers to author Sarah J. Maas as "the queen of fairy smut" – in a recent headline for an article discussing the mega-popularity of the series and merch sales. In fairness to The Times, the article does clarify that the "queen of fairy smut" phrasing that they're quoting is used "lovingly" by some of Maas' fans, when describing her (as opposed to The Times describing her as such). Regardless, it hits different to see Sarah J. Maas referred to in that way in a headline, knowing it'll be read by people outside the fandom. And it ties into the bigger topic, which is that the term being used -- even in an affectionate or humorous way -- to describe the author and her series might create the impression that the main draw of these books, which are massively popular among women, is the fairy sex.

The first ACOTAR book sees the primary protagonist, Feyre Archeron, taken captive by a beastly fae male after she kills a wolf while trying to hunt for food to feed her family. This draws her into the magic realm that she and other humans typically avoid due to the danger. Romance and adventure ensue from there, and more characters are added or developed further as the books go on. I think there's only one descriptive sex scene in the first book. The spice increases in later books, but so does the number of pages. Are we all really reading 700+ page fantasy books for the occasional bit of erotica?

I'm not going to sit here and tell you that the spice isn't part of what's great about the ACOTAR books, but it's by no means the first thing I'd celebrate about it. I actually think it'd be misrepresenting the books to recommend them to someone looking for an especially spicy romantasy series.

My main takeaways from all of the ACOTAR books have to do with bigger developments in the story – epic battles, magical abilities, weapons with special powers, scary or mysterious beings dwelling in the forest or mountains or the bottom of a lake. You know, the stuff you might find in fantasy novels? I do love the way romance is woven in with the magic – how a mating bond can create a deep connection between two fae. Romantasy is undoubtedly a fair description for these books, as is the case with Maas' other series (Throne of Glass, Crescent City). "Fairy smut" is not.

One thing I absolutely love about the ACOTAR books is the complexity of their female characters and often the sisterhood they find (both with actual sisters and chosen family). Sure, these heroines have romantic interests, but they're also battling inner demons, facing drastic changes in their lives, making choices, reckoning with their past traumas, and coming into their power. It's exciting! It's emotional and suspenseful, and it leaves me simultaneously satisfied and wanting more. That they fall in love and have great sex amidst everything else going on is undoubtedly part of the draw (if the ACOTAR TV show happens, I'd absolutely want the romance and spiciness to be a part of it), but it's just one piece of a greater epic story.

I think my reason for wanting to say this all out loud – beyond listening to other fans on Instagram expressing their own thoughts and frustration and defending Sarah J. Maas for her accomplishments – is that I love seeing the ACOTAR books receive the praise and love they deserve (including from celebrities like Margot Robbie and even Anne Hathaway), as evidenced by how excited people are about the new books. I'm one of the many fans who got on board with Maas' books after A Court of Silver Flames came out, after all. When something breaks out into the mainstream as ACOTAR has, people start to wonder what it is that fans -- again, in many cases with this one, women -- love about it. The answer to that is a lot of things, including great storytelling on the author's part.

To brand it smut, even in an affectionate or jokey way, especially if you're speaking to or from outside the fandom, reduces the series to one thing, and it's not even the main thing I and many other fans love the most about it.

Kelly put her life-long love of movies, TV and books to greater use when she joined CinemaBlend as a freelance TV news writer in 2006, and went on to serve as the site’s TV Editor before joining the staff full-time in 2011 and moving over to other roles at the site. At present, she’s an Assistant Managing Editor who spends much of her time brainstorming and editing features, analyzing site data, working with writers and editors on content planning and the workflow, and obsessing over the best movies and TV shows. She graduated from SUNY Cortland with BA in Communication Studies and a minor in Cinema Studies. When she isn't working, she's probably thinking about work, or reading (or listening to a book), and making sure her cats are living their absolute best feline lives.

#3684. Oprah Winfrey Answers the Proust Questionnaire

A rainy day, a fireplace, a great book, and 300 pages to go.

Which historical figure do you most identify with?

What is the trait you most deplore in others?

Seven parties in seven days for Maya Angelou’s 70th birthday.

What do you regard as the lowest depth of misery?

If you could change one thing about yourself, what would it be?

To be less judgmental and more confrontational.

Not taking a year off after ending The Oprah Show and jumping right into runninga network.

All-time? Filming The Color Purple in 1985, hosting the Legends Ball for African American She-roes, and Christmas Kindness 2002, where we surprised thousands of kids throughout South Africa with gifts.

What Glinda the Good Witch said: “You’ve always had the power.”

What do you dislike most about your appearance?

What or who is the greatest love of your life?

The Oprah Show, and all 21 dogs I’ve had throughout my life, who’ve taught me so much about living and dying.

Chewing gum—and people who chew with their mouths open, showing the gum. Ugh!

What do you consider your greatest achievement?

Creating spaces where people could see themselves more clearly and recognize the best of who they are.

If you were to die and come back as a person or thing, what do you think it would be?

My first-edition Pulitzer Prize books, dating back to 1918; slave rosters with the names and ages of each enslaved person in the household; and six charcoal drawings Nelson Mandela drew from prison. He called me into his office and gave them to me by hand.

Ordinary folks who do extraordinary things: what author Dacher Keltner calls acts of moral beauty.

As the traditional African American spiritual goes: “I wanna die easy when I die / Shout salvation as I fly.”

#3683. Marvel 1943 ‘Has Not Been Canceled,’ Says Skydance Leadership, Despite Development Struggles

Today, a rumor began to spread that Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was about to be canceled. But according to a source on the project, developers are being reassured that it is not, in fact, canceled, despite ongoing struggles.

The news of a cancelation announcement was first spread by fan account Marvel 1943 Rise Of Hydra Countdown, and was quickly picked up in fan circles. However, before it could be confirmed or elaborated upon, executive producer Lu Gigliotti posted a message in the Skydance Slack (viewed by Kotaku) stating that he had spoken “directly” with the “executive leadership team (Dan [Prigg], Shawn [Kittelson], Andrea [Benavides], etc.) [all Skydance employees]” and that the game was not canceled. “They asked me to make sure you all hear that directly. There is no truth to these claims.” Developers were told not to let the rumor distract them, and that the studio was “monitoring the situation” and would address it “through the appropriate channels.”

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was begun as Amy Hennig’s project within the newly established Skydance New Media in 2019. It was teased in 2022 and fully revealed in 2024, with plans to release in holiday of 2025. The game would have been an action-adventure starring Captain America, Black Panther, Gabriel Jones, and Nanali as they take down the budding terrorist organization Hydra.

According to the Slack post, the game is approaching an “Alpha” milestone later this month, though Kotaku understands it has run into significant, repeated trouble throughout its development. Marvel 1943 was first delayed to “beyond early 2026” and then further delayed into 2027 and beyond. The original pitch for Marvel 1943 was as a Netflix game, but it transitioned to a console and PC game during development. As a result, its current rendition is light on gameplay, primarily using only one button and lacking significant interaction. It is also well over budget, and has been significantly cut back from its original vision both in terms of length and content. Kotaku’s source says the project is now “close to done.”

Just two days ago, at least 30 people at Paramount Games were laid off in the wake of the merger between Paramount and Warner Bros., Those impacted included many from Skydance, though the exact number remains unclear, and it does not appear to have had significant impact on the Marvel 1943 team.

Kotaku has reached out to both Skydance and Marvel for comment.

#3682. Brandy and Monica Tease Joint Las Vegas Residency Will Be on 'Another Level'

Brandy and Monica are ready to roll the dice and take fans back to the ‘90s with their upcoming joint Las Vegas residency.

“This is going to be another level,” Brandy, 47, exclusively told Us on Tuesday, November 10, after performing alongside Monica, 46, during Dancing With the Stars’ Grammy Night.

The musician teased that the residency, which comes after their 2025 The Boy Is Mine Tour, will be “elevated and just great and phenomenal, and I’m just so excited.”

Brandy added that she “can’t wait to get to work” on the 10-show experience ahead of the tour kickoff over Memorial Day weekend in 2027.

“We have a lot to prepare for, but we look forward to it,” Monica revealed, noting that she and Brandy “really start to create when we get together.”

She promised that the pair will get into Resorts World Las Vegas and “make it an experience” that fans won’t soon forget.

“[We’ll] make sure we take them into what it was like to be a part of music from 1994 up until this very moment,” Monica told Us.

Brandy and Monica initially collaborated on “The Boy Is Mine” in 1988. The duet was featured on both artist’s second studio albums, Brandy’s Never Say Never and Monica’s The Boy Is Mine.

The track and its accompanying music video made a massive splash in the music industry, being nominated for two MTV Video Music Awards, including Video of the Year and Best R&B Video.

The song won a Grammy for Best R&B Vocal Performance by a Duo or Group and received two other nominations in 1999.

Monica and Brandy reunited in 2012 to record the “It All Belongs to Me” single. They also made a cameo in Ariana Grande’s 2024 music video for her song “The Boy Is Mine,” which is a reimagining of the ‘90s classic.

Amid the song’s resurgence, Brandy and Monica embarked on their The Boy Is Mine Tour, which ran from October to December 2025 across the U.S.

It was revealed during Tuesday’s DWTS that Brandy and Monica will be coheadlining The Boy Is Mine residency in Las Vegas. The shows will take place in Resorts World Theatre beginning on May 29, 2027 and will run through July 17, 2027.

When asked why fans are craving all-things ‘90s, including their music, Brandy told Us, “Because the ’90s is where it’s at. It’s the best. I just feel like that’s where it’s at.”

The Moesha alum pointed out, “The most incredible artists came out in the ’90s. Whitney [Houston] was in the ’90s. Mariah Carey‘s in the ’90s.”

Monica couldn’t agree more, saying that all the ‘90s artists were “individuals” who flourished in their respective lanes.

“We all had our own sound, our own vibes, and it was so welcomed. It wasn’t where everything sounded the same,” she recalled. “That’s what I think people are craving, those differences and those nuances between all of us that made us all so different.”

Monica added that by teaming up with Brandy, fans will get the best of both worlds — past and present.

“Coming together, it just brings you to that moment two times over,” she concluded. “So that’s how we want people to feel when they come to Resorts World.”

Tickets for The Boy Is Mine residency go on sale Friday, November 20.

Dancing With the Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET.
