#3681. Johnny Depp on Honoring Hunter S. Thompson’s Final Wish With a “Death Cannon” That Stood “Taller Than the Statue of Liberty”

He couldn’t remember if it was day or night when he found it, in the place where “one never quite knew or cared for time,” Johnny Depp wrote. He remembered the year—1997—and that he was with Hunter S. Thompson in his basement War Room at Owl Farm. It was just across the hall from Depp’s bedroom, with that old keg of dynamite serving as his bedside table.

Rummaging through beaten-up boxes that comprised Thompson’s archive, Depp unearthed something that would turn out to be equally explosive. “A battered typescript,” he called it. Abandoned among the detritus of Thompson’s renegade life, it was “bound together by rubber bands.” On its cover, “in Hunter’s own hand,” Depp noted, were the words THE RUM DIARY.

“He wrote the book in his early twenties,” Depp wrote. “And then stuffed it away.”

Side by side on the floor of the War Room, Depp and Thompson began “reading it to one another.” And when they were done, Depp had made a decision: “The Rum Diary was simply too good to remain lost.”

Thompson wasn’t able to find a publisher for The Rum Diary when it was written, but now he was, well, Hunter S. Thompson. With Depp as his advocate, The Rum Diary was published in 1998. “Almost immediately, the subject of a film was broached,” Depp wrote in a foreword to the screenplay, recalling Thompson saying, “‘Hot damn . . . yessir, let’s you and I produce this caper together, Colonel! We’ll have Hollywood groveling at our feet! They will crawl over a road of bones to get to us! Yessir!’”

A movie didn’t happen “as easily as we had hoped,” Depp continued in his foreword. “Fiery hoops of all dimensions, covert bear traps, woefully obstinate billfolds” arose in their path, “which neither Hunter or I were remotely experienced in battling . . . But we weren’t giving up.”

Hunter S. Thompson at his ranch in Colorado, 1990.

As the years wore on, Thompson grew increasingly inflamed over the development hell of Hollywood, writing producer Holly Sorensen a fiery missive in January 2001: “Dear Holly, Okay, you lazy bitch, I’m getting tired of this waterhead fuckaround that you’re doing with The Rum Diary. We are not even spinning our wheels aggressively. It’s like the whole Project got turned over to Zombies who live in cardboard boxes under the Hollywood Freeway. I seem to be the only person who’s doing anything about getting this movie Made. I have rounded up Depp, Benicio del Toro, Brad Pitt, Nick Nolte and a fine screenwriter from England named Michael Thomas.”

The eventual screenwriter for The Rum Diary turned out to be Bruce Robinson, the British director of the twisted 1987 cult classic Withnail and I, which both Depp and Thompson were “mutually obsessed with.” Depp had originally asked Robinson to direct the film adaptation of Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas—but by then, Robinson had quit directing, wrung out by the Hollywood system that had subjected him to making the Uma Thurman–led thriller Jennifer 8 for Paramount. He was content to spend the rest of his life writing screenplays and books and had vowed to never direct a movie again.

In 2005, Johnny tracked Robinson down while he was on vacation in Spain. “Have you read The Rum Diary?” Depp asked. Bruce hadn’t. The next day there was a knock on Robinson’s hotel room door, along with “the book The Rum Diary that Johnny had sent,” said Robinson.

“I wasn’t impressed by the book,” he continued. Neither were most critics: “For someone who gets to drink rum all day and have sex on the beach (the real thing, not the cocktail) all night, Kemp is pretty morose,” wrote one reviewer of the Thompson character. Despite some early incantations of the hellish voice that Thompson used with such tremendous force later in his career, it had many of the problems that plague early attempts at fiction. But because it was Johnny Depp, Robinson said he would try his hand at writing the screenplay.

Once back in Herefordshire, however, he found he could not write. Not a single word. “Nothing, nothing, nothing,” he said.

He knew the problem: abstinence. “I think it’s called alcoholism, probably,” he said of his tolerance for red wine. He had been sober for six and a half years, before which he had been “literally drinking wine all day while I worked. I’d finally gotten to the point where I was tired of doing that every day, seven days a week, so I cut the booze out of my life completely.”

Now he was stuck. Without the wine, which he said unleashed him from the gridlock of his superego, he was blocked. “You know I’m just going to have to drink some wine for this,” he finally confided to his wife. With her blessings, he opened a bottle of red, and then another and another, “one bottle of red wine a day—every day—for the three months it took me to write the story,” he said.

Then, as he was almost done with the screenplay (along with the Bordeaux), he drove into town to get the Sunday papers. The news was all over his radio: the American writer and journalist Hunter S. Thompson had killed himself.

“Oh, my God,” Robinson thought. “That’s the end of the movie.”

Hunter S. Thompson takes on his ranch in Colorado, 1976

Sunday, February 20, 2005. A heavy rainstorm lashed the streets of Los Angeles. Mist clung to the palms and a sense of gloom fell over the city, as it always does when it rains in L.A. Christi Dembrowski turned off Sunset and drove up the winding road to her brother’s home, bearing news that she knew would break Johnny’s heart: Hunter S. Thompson had died that afternoon of a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head.

“My sister Christi turned up at the house in a pouring rainstorm,” Depp said. “She’d received a phone call two hours after it had happened and didn’t want me to see it on CNN. She told me Hunter had gone. But as much of a shock as it was, as much horror as I felt when you receive such blunt, bad news, I also knew Hunter was never going to be the guy who was going to collapse in a bowl of soup.”

After the shock—along with the eulogies for the fallen writer dominating airwaves, telephone lines, and barrooms worldwide—came what Depp called the “devastation.”

“Tragic,” he told Tom Thurman in the 2006 documentary Buy the Ticket, Take the Ride: Hunter S. Thompson on Film. “Shocked but not shocked. Angry but understanding. A zillion different emotions flying around all the time. It was like somebody had removed something from your body. It was a heavy hit.”

Mourning the loss of his brother, mentor, hero, and friend, Johnny’s mind flashed back to the 1978 BBC documentary Fear and Loathing in Gonzovision, in which Thompson described in minute detail how he would like to be sent off from this world into the next: he wanted his remains cremated and shot from a cannon on his land in Woody Creek, Colorado.

“When I got the news that Hunter had made his exit, obviously I was devastated,” Depp said. “I remember thinking almost immediately, ‘The cannon. We’ve got to do the cannon.’”

For Depp, this wasn’t a writer’s fantasy; it was Thompson’s final command. “That bastard,” Depp said. “I know somewhere in his crooked mind . . . he knew that I was the only one perhaps loyal enough, perhaps insane enough, to attempt it.”

Over the years, Thompson had spoken about what would be called “the death cannon,” Depp said. “You know, he brought it up every now and again; ‘Oh, yeah, I’ve got to have—I need the cannon, you know. . . . I may have even said, ‘I’ll send you off.’”

Thompson’s son, Juan, was determined to make it happen, too. Only Juan envisioned a twelve-foot cannon, costing a couple of hundred dollars. Johnny wanted something bigger, grander. “A few days later, Doug Brinkley, Hunter’s good friend and editor of his letters books, came over to our cabin and said Johnny Depp had called and said he wanted to pay for the construction of the cannon,” Juan wrote in his 2016 memoir Stories I Tell Myself: Growing Up with Hunter S. Thompson. “We were astonished . . . it is one thing to be a friend; it’s another thing to volunteer to build a friend’s death cannon.

An initial commemoration of Thompson’s life was held at the Hotel Jerome in Aspen on March 5, 2005. It was “essentially a party with music, photos and videos, interspersed with testimonials from friends and family,” Juan wrote. Depp flew to Aspen with Benicio del Toro and John Cusack to attend it. During the event, one of Depp’s assistants found Juan in the crowd “and asked me to come with him to Johnny’s room,” Juan wrote.

The assistant “slowly opened the door. And I entered the dark room and looked around, and in the center of the bed was a sculpture, lit from within. A giant boom box was playing Norman Greenbaum’s “Spirit in the Sky,” with its lyrics, “When I lay me down to die / Goin’ up to the spirit in the sky.”

“The sculpture was a tapering silver tower made of aluminum, about three feet high, topped by a blood-red fist,” Juan remembered. “The two-thumbed fist. The peyote button glowed from within with shifting colors. There was a small hole in the top of the fist where the projectile would exit.”

It was a magnificent miniature model that exceeded even Hunter Thompson’s wildest dreams. The full version, as envisioned by Johnny, would be “153 feet tall, 15 stories, taller even than what Hunter imagined,” wrote Juan. “Taller than the Statue of Liberty.”

The cannon would be fabricated in Los Angeles and hauled in pieces to Owl Farm on flatbed trucks. “It has to be perfect,” Depp told his long-time contractor, Steve Cohn, who coordinated the event over three months in Aspen (residing in three suites in three different Aspen hotels; at one of them, the Sky Hotel, Cohn allegedly set the record on room service booze and “incidentals,” spending more than $100,000). No expense was spared for what would become a monumental undertaking, requiring six months of massive set designing, and construction and engineering crews “numbering at least a hundred” from Hollywood and beyond, said Cohn.

On August 20, 2005, a crowd of 250, including Jack Nicholson, Sean Penn, Bill Murray, and Senators George McGovern and John Kerry, assembled on the meadow behind Thompson’s home. After the toasts and speeches (“Hunter, this is for you,” said Depp), a video clip of Thompson discussing his funeral cannon in his 1978 BBC interview was played on a giant screen. A Japanese drum ensemble began performing. Glasses of champagne were passed around. Then all eyes were on the massive cannon, its red fabric curtains unfurling to reveal the gonzo logo—the two-thumbed fist and the pulsating green peyote button—at the top of the 153-foot tower. “Spirit in the Sky” blasted from the speakers. “Then, at 8:46 p.m., more than thirty fireworks rocketed high above Owl Farm . . .” Doug Brinkley wrote in Rolling Stone. “The cannon atop the tower fired, and Hunter’s ashes fell over the assembled guests like gray snow. ‘Mr. Tambourine Man’ blaring from the sound system on cue. Hunter was literally all around us now. . . . ‘I have never seen an event like this,’ whispered the actor Harry Dean Stanton. ‘And I’m old. Very old.’”

“Everybody was speechless,” said Cohn. “Johnny and I were sitting together when it went off. He looked at me, smiled, and said, ‘That was awesome.’”

With Thompson’s ashes in the air, the party began in a massive tent decorated to look like Hunter’s kitchen and living room.

Bruce Robinson’s initial thought was that the death of Hunter Thompson would mean the death of The Rum Diary. But he was wrong about that.

“I had lost my dear friend and co-conspirator,” Depp wrote. “Sure as fuck wasn’t going to give up now.”

#3679. Love Is Blind's Sarah Shares New Claims About John's 'Explicit' Escort Texts

Love Is Blind season 11 star Sarah Williams claims she saw the “sexually explicit” texts her estranged husband, John Shannon, admittedly sent to a stripper who also works as an escort during their marriage.

“When I saw the text messages, which was, as far as I know, it was just this one person in the text that I saw,” Sarah, 34, alleged on the Wednesday, November 11, episode of “The Viall Files” podcast. “She was reminding him that she’s an escort. I later found out that she was the stripper that they met at the strip club. … She was like, ‘I’m an escort. You got to pay me.’”

Sarah and John, 33, were the sole couple to say “I do” in the season 11 finale, though their marriage broke down nearly one year later. John revealed during the Sunday, November 8, reunion that he made a “mistake” that ultimately signified the end of their marriage by exchanging a few racy texts with a stripper — but denied that anything physical happened. (Sarah has stated that she also left their marriage for other reasons, including losing confidence in herself and the problematic way her husband allegedly spoke to her when mad or overwhelmed.)

While detailing the alleged correspondence on the “Viall Files” podcast, Sarah claimed that she found “sexually explicit requests” between John and the unidentified sex worker.

“Then the texts stop, and there’s no evidence of connection or physical cheating,” she said, agreeing with host Nick Viall’s assumption that John was “engaging with [the escort] like a civilian” with the hope of potentially establishing a romantic relationship in the future.

While Sarah acknowledged that John is “his own person,” he admitted his emotional infidelity directly.

“John and I had an open phone policy, but I’ve never been through his phone,” she said. “ I found out because on boy trips, I’m fine with the strip club, like, it’s fine. And we explicitly talked about it. I was like, ‘Yeah, if you go and the guys go, that’s totally OK, just behave [and] don’t be weird about it.’”

Despite Sarah allowing John to go on the trip, she still says he lied about his attendance when further pressed.

“He lied for no reason because we had talked about it and I was like, ‘No, you can go.’ So then that triggered something in my brain,” Sarah added. “I was like, ‘Oh, he lied about the trip. That’s weird.’ And then, it was very laid out for me. It was very easy [to find in his phone].”

In addition to scouring John’s past messages, Sarah also allegedly saw that he had downloaded the dating app Tinder.

“All this is at like 3:00 a.m., mind you, but like I don’t care. I don’t care that, there was intention, and even if you were wasted, you had wasted intention. It’s gross,” Sarah claimed, further alleging that John’s profile had “a match” at the time she discovered his account. “Maybe he’s always had it and it was deactivated or something and he just activated [it]. I don’t know.”

Sarah, who claimed that John even accused her of infidelity months before revealing his texting scandal, subsequently confronted her then-spouse.

“I don’t think he took me seriously at first,” she said on Wednesday’s episode, also claiming that John said he didn’t use the app outside of his boys’ trip where he met the escort. “He says no and nothing physical happened and that, after the texting and stuff, he wanted to come home ‘cause that’s when he realized he liked being married.”

Sarah ultimately filed for divorce in June, citing an irretrievable breakdown of their marriage.

#3678. Hey, Nintendo, What’s Going On With Zelda: Ocarina Of Time’s Most Insufferable Couple?

Nintendo Switch 2The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

I’ve been gushing for a few days now about some of the smaller details added to Hyrule in the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, like this new dialogue in Castle Town and new clarity on the fate of the Zora. But last night I ran into another deeply silly addition that I just have to tell you about. It’s controversy! Scandal! Confusion?

What the heck is going on with Honey and Darling?

If you don’t know who Honey and Darling are, you’ve definitely seen them before. They’re the perpetually dancing couple who appear in the center square of Hyrule Castle Town, and then move to the hilltop behind the windmill in Kakariko Village in the adult era. In the original Ocarina of Time, they are unnamed, but Majora’s Mask canonized their alternate selves as Honey and Darling. Ocarina of Time has them using those same nicknames for one another, so in the interest of clarity, I’m going to refer to them here, too, as Honey (the woman) and Darling (the man).

Honey and Darling are iconic and insufferable. In the original game, they sit there and gush over how in love they are with one another, with Honey comparing Darling to the handsome King of Hyrule and Darling saying Honey is more beautiful than Princess Zelda. They continue spinning on and on into the night, day after day. In Kakariko, they’reÂ still spinning, offering Link no useful information when he speaks to them but instead calling him “annoying” and accusing him of “violating” their “personal space.” If you approach them wearing one of the game’s many masks, they still express nothing more interesting than irritation with you for daring to exist. Rude! I just wanted to chat!

From all that, you can interpret little more than that Honey and Darling are obsessively in love with one another, get some sort of kick out of publicly displaying that love, and are still together in spite of their mutual insufferability (or perhaps because of it) seven years later. Fine, unremarkable.

In the remake, though! This pair is back, seemingly the same as ever, albeit with some more dialogue that has each of them gushing over their respective partner. Nothing to see here, right? Wrong.Â Put on that Mask of Truth!

The Mask of Truth is an item received from the Happy Mask Salesman sidequests that, when donned, allows you to read the minds of most characters. Unlike in the original, here you can wear masks as both child and adult Link, which gives you double the opportunities to see what’s really going on in people’s heads. The Mask of Truth dialogue adds a lot of humor and context to many of the game’s interactions, but in the case of Honey and Darling, it has utterly baffled me. Get a load of this:

That’s Darling speaking! What! What the hell, man?! You don’t even know this woman’s name and you’ve been spinning around this square declaring your love for her for how long? How many other women are you seeing? Sheesh! When paired with Honey’s dialogue posted above (“If he ever hurts me, I’ll never forgive him…”), this suggests something a little ominous for the future of their relationship, right?

So let’s check in on them in Kakariko Village, seven years in the future. Still dancing, still obsessing over one another. Except…

Excuse me?! That’s Honey speaking this time! The younger twin ofÂ whom?! As far as I’m aware, Honey having a twin has never once come up. Unless…okay, I’m putting it together here. Darling is dating a pair of twin sisters. He knows they’re twins, but can’t keep their names straight. Honey (and Honey 2, I guess) are also aware of this arrangement and don’t care, but the younger of the two seems a bit dismayed that Darling can’t tell them apart.

I’ve been trying to do reporter work all day, looking around both towns for a double of Honey hiding somewhere, but I’ve come up empty. I’ve tried Mask of Truthing everyone in the vicinity to see if anyone knows anything about what’s happening here and will comment on it, but it’s no good. I am left with only theories as to what sort of bizarre relationship is going on between these two, maybe three, people. You might say, “Reb, this is none of your business!” To that I say, Honey and Honey and Darling made it my business when they started dramatically parading their romance in the town square. For all of their sakes, however many of them there are, I hope every member of this relationship is clued in as to the presence of every other person within it. Otherwise, I’m predicting some serious scandal come Majora’s Mask time.

Major spoilers for the VisionQuest finale lie ahead.

I've learned never to trust a Marvel character's death, especially when that death involves a conveniently placed pile of rubble. After the VisionQuest finale dropped one hell of a surprise involving Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch, I've been thinking about something she told CinemaBlend four years ago. With Avengers: Doomsday approaching on the 2026 movie schedule, her comments about the X-Men suddenly seem a whole lot more interesting.

Back in May 2022, CinemaBlend interviewed Olsen about Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness and asked whether she'd be interested in exploring Wanda Maximoff's comic book connections to the X-Men. At the time, Olsen wasn't sure what Marvel had planned for her character, but our question apparently got her pretty excited. Check out the video below, posted to our official Instagram account:

A post shared by CinemaBlend (@cinemablend)

Well, four years later, the X-Men are officially part of Marvel's immediate future, and Wanda's situation has changed considerably. So, does that mean Olsen's dream could come true? As she put it:

But I guess you just said it, if we're bringing X-Men back, I'll wanna be there!

The X-Men are back, along with seemingly every other Marvel character, and if the actress has her way, she wants to be there- and who's gonna tell her no? Before we get into why that interview deserves another look, consider yourself warned.

In the VisionQuest finale, "Forever," the main story ends on a surprisingly sweet note. Tommy Maximoff, who's been a supporting character throughout the series, finally reunites with his brother Billy, who makes his return to help his brother revive their father after his system nearly shuts. Vision ultimately embraces his two boys, and the Maximoff family finally comes back together after everything that happened in WandaVision. But there's still somebody missing.

Near the end, Tommy directly asks Vision whether they might ever see Wanda again. Vision offers a hopeful answer, recalling that they've said goodbye before, so perhaps they can say hello again. It's an unexpectedly touching moment, particularly when you remember where we last saw her. Then the second post-credits scene practically answers Tommy's question.

We return to Mount Wundagore, where Wanda appeared to sacrifice herself at the end of Multiverse of Madness after realizing the destruction she'd caused. Doctor Doom arrives, removes the rubble and awakens the Scarlet Witch. She gasps back to life, while Doom makes it clear he's interested in her extraordinary powers. Marvel really knows how to make you sit through the credits, doesn't it?

We were already theorizing about Scarlet Witch's possible involvement in Doomsday back in September, following rumors that Wanda could play a significant role in the upcoming Avengers movie. Well, I imagine those theories are about to get considerably more interesting.

The second post-credit scene also serves as an obvious bridge to Avengers: Doomsday, arriving Dec. 18. Marvel has confirmed that Ian McKellen's Magneto and Patrick Stewart's Professor X are among the returning X-Men actors. Wanda's comic book history is tangled up with mutants, including her former connection to Magneto as his daughter, a relationship Marvel later retconned.

None of that confirms Olsen will share a scene with Magneto, or even how Doom plans to use Wanda. But hearing her light up over the prospect of X-Men stories four years ago feels particularly fun now. Personally, I'm hoping the Maximoffs get their family reunion before the next catastrophe. But if Marvel also wants to revisit this old question about the Charles Xavier's mutants, I'll be paying attention.

A Major Avengers Return Was Just Set Up In VisionQuest, But I Have Another Doomsday Question

Marvel is bringing several original X-Men actors back for the upcoming Avengers movie, including Ian McKellen as Magneto and the late Patrick Stewart as Professor X, in his final on-screen performance. And anyone familiar with Wanda's comic book history knows why that first name is especially interesting.

In the comics, Wanda and her brother Pietro were Magneto's children, at least until Marvel decided to rewrite that particular family tree. But in the House of M story run, Wanda nearly wiped out the entire mutant population. And wouldn't you know it, Olsen has actually said she'd love to see that storyline adapted. Given everything happening with the X-Men, I can't help wondering if Marvel might finally give her the opportunity.

Of course, we're getting ahead of ourselves. We still don't know what Doctor Doom wants with Wanda, much less whether she'll cross paths with Magneto. But it's pretty funny looking back at our 2022 interview now. Olsen was already excited about getting involved with the X-Men, and four years later, Marvel has brought her character back just as the mutants are entering the picture. I'd love to know what she thinks about that timing.

#3676. Dolly Parton Is Gone, But Dollywood Will Always Love Her

“RIP Dolly Smoky Mountain Angel” was one of the first signs we saw as we pulled up on the side of a motel in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. Just down the same road was another memorial to her on a Burger King sign. This was in early October. Dolly Parton, the country singer and actor, widely considered a Great American Who Everyone Loves, had died, at the age of 80, in late August. I am not the kind of person who cries over celebrity deaths, but after I heard that she died, I went to my closet to find a Dolly Parton T-shirt I had bought the one time I saw her live, at a concert of mostly acoustic songs in Queens in 2016. I couldn’t find it. I blamed my brief flirtation with the Marie Kondo method, but there was no way that T-shirt hadn’t sparked joy.

Early October in Sevier County, in far eastern Tennessee, where Parton was born, is full of cabins on some parcels of land that dot the ancient Appalachians. But among the rolling green expanses are Mexican supermarkets, coffee shops, apple orchards, and pumpkin patches. This is where she opened the amusement park Dollywood in 1986. The Great Smoky Mountains National Park draws masses about 13 miles from Dollywood. The fancier of my friends identified the area as where the Blackberry Farm resort is. But Pigeon Forge has a feeling of a Jersey Shore boardwalk in Appalachia, with a strip of businesses that sell vapes and ATV rides and Moon Pies a block from a Margaritaville hotel.

Parton opened Dollywood in 1986 at the foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains. Today, it draws in millions of people annually—loving fans who don her iconic pink cowboy hat or accessories honoring the park's famous Grist Mill Cinnamon Bread (a cult favorite).

Locals heap the kind of praise on Parton that we’ve come to expect knowing her reputation as a goddess among mortals. “People don’t understand what she did for this place and meant to this place. She threw lots of money at it and went out of her way to take care of this place,” an Uber driver named Eric told me as we exited the highway into Dollywood, with its script logo and “love every moment” greeting signs. “I got to meet her three times at the park because she would just show up and stand there with a crowd of people. For someone who’s been famous as long as she’s been famous you’d expect a certain air of haughtiness,” he says. “But I was stunned at how kind she was.”

Parton’s job title at the park was dreamer-in-chief, and part of Dollywood’s allure is that it’s a shrine to her life and career. There’s a replica of the two-room wood cabin where she grew up a sharecropper’s daughter, in close quarters alongside her parents and 10 siblings. Her home, not even 500 square feet, had no electricity nor running water. (The original home still stands about 10 miles away but isn’t open to the public.)

Parton wrote the country ballad “I Will Always Love You” in 1973 as a heartfelt farewell to her longtime business partner Porter Wagoner. Now, fans honoring Dolly's memory have used the slogan for the park's new annual festival, which opens in March 2027.

That modest beginning is plenty known, but Dollywood also celebrates Parton as she became a household name and wildly rich. The Dolly Parton Experience is a museum devoted to her trajectory, from Nashville ingenue to a celebrity among celebrities (photos show her with Mick Jagger in the ’60s and Whitney Houston in the ’90s). It has a gallery devoted to her Imagination Library, which has donated more than 300 million books to children around the world. Another building across a landscaped path celebrates her role in the workplace revenge comedy 9 to 5 (September 25 has now been christened a holiday in Sevier County) and houses a half dozen of her wigs, sorted by decade, all platinum, all voluminous. A plaque commemorates her wig stylists, starting with her Aunt Colleen. Parton’s costumes are scattered around the tributes, including a black flared jumpsuit with a hot pink shirt and neck ruffle so intense it looks Elizabethan. One wall features one of Parton’s famously self-effacing quotes: “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap.”

In her mobile home, which guests line up around to take a tour, she has a closet with a hanging yellow diamanté dress, a full-size bathtub because she preferred baths to showers, mirrored ceilings because she was claustrophobic, and cheeky digital clocks that display her most hallowed time zones: Dollywood (5:53 p.m. ET) and Nashville (4:53 p.m. CT). I ask our tour guide, a woman in a sparkly vest, how she and the park employees have fared without Parton. “Today is the first day I haven’t cried,” she admits.

Dollywood is more than a museum—it's an amusement park. The 165-acre Pigeon Forge carnival features over 50 rides and Dollywood's Splash Country, a 35-acre water park.

But more than a museum, Dollywood is an amusement park, and a much bigger one than I had realized. It’s a place where you can stand in line for 45 minutes to buy a corn dog while listening to a four-person singing-and-dancing group in the vein of the Mickey Mouse Club does peppy but half-assed covers of Fleetwood Mac and Van Halen. Looping rollercoasters and water tube rides leave families soaking wet in matching T-shirts commemorating their vacations. Dondre, my colleague and our photographer for this journey, waits probably a full hour to squeeze into a vintage muscle car with me so I can simulate steering around a track. It wasn’t until deep into our wait time that we realize this is a children’s ride. At this point, the two of us notice that, in the sea of people, we are the only ones who are childless, wearing dark colors, and audibly bemoaning that Dollywood is dry. (Parton was not a strict teetotaler, but the park bills itself as assertively family-friendly. “Weapons and alcoholic beverages are not permitted on Dollywood Property” is the only explanation given on its website.) No one else seems to care. The ride is quick, but we are ecstatic, high on refillable Diet Cokes, kettle corn, and driving a car, which neither one of us knows how to do in real life.

Some park employees have not fared well without Parton. One tour guide admits: “Today is the first day I haven’t cried." Parton passed away on August 25 at the age of 80 after a battle with cancer.

We don’t want real life at Dollywood. We want the dreamer-in-chief’s dreams. For dinner, we hit the 8:30 show of Dolly Parton’s Stampede in Pigeon Forge, an equestrian version of dinner theater where guests are served a whole chicken, pulled pork, corn, greens, a biscuit, pie, and unlimited soda, all to be eaten by hand while the not so vague perfume of manure wafts through the air. Horses with cowboys and cowgirls astride them jump through rings of fire, someone does wire work while dangling from the ceiling, and American flags fly in abundance. We catch a pig race. Sooo-ey! At another point, a volunteer from the audience disappears from a barrel before our eyes. The whole thing feels psychedelic, and we peak when performers in butterfly wings ride around to Parton’s song “Love Is Like a Butterfly.” I squeal as a few actual buffalo take the arena. After the show, I ask a cowboy how the majestic creatures are as animal coworkers, and he shakes his head. “There’s a reason I stick to horses.”

Even in the perfect bubble of Dollywood, in the wake of her death, Parton’s spirit has already faded into the nostalgia.

There isn’t enough acknowledgement of Parton’s death at the park for my taste; no candlelit vigil or impersonators we can hug. By the second day, my mania has subsided, giving way to contemplation. I ask fellow parkgoers if they have come to pay respects. Every single one replies that their trip has been planned long before. My attempts to make small talk with strangers doesn’t result in the fantasy of one collective mourning. Families in seasonal T-shirts seem shy and uninterested in chatting with me, a strangely inquisitive middle-aged woman who wants to ask them if they’ve heard the rumor that Dolly Parton was secretly covered in tattoos. (They haven’t.) A friend group of two lesbian couples from Pennsylvania brushes off my line of questioning around whether Parton might have been more than just queer-friendly (rainbow Dollywood shirts and backpacks and trucker caps are for sale). Too soon, they say, and shake their heads—too salacious to be airing gossip. I ask other strangers if they have heard the family drama over Parton’s estate. Most dismiss me, but another Uber driver, this one named Austin, says, “She has a huge estate and a big family, and it was always going to happen. We’ll see how it plays out.” (In November, the lawsuit was dropped, and Parton’s nephew said he was happy to put the issue behind him.)

The butterfly is a key part of Dollywood's logo, representing Parton's personal emblem. As a little girl growing up in the Smoky Mountains, she was fascinated by butterflies and related to their gentle grace. She cemented the motif into her career in 1974 with the hit song, “Love is Like a Butterfly.”

Maybe, I say to Dondre, no one will talk to me because I, unlike about 50% of the people there, am not wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with a Bible verse, a military slogan, or a celebration of America’s 250 years. I keep pointing out paintings of crosses and eagles and American flags—often all combined on one canvas together—for sale. Dondre says, in a kind way, that nothing is more cliché than hearing someone from New York talk about other parts of the country. Maybe what made Dolly Parton so winning—her apparent lack of judgment—is not something I inherently have. It can’t hurt to try to be a little more like Parton in our own daily lives.

Maybe she had an optimism no one can ever replace. And that’s ultimately okay because you can try to channel that anywhere. Even in the perfect bubble of Dollywood, in the wake of her death, Parton’s spirit has already faded into the nostalgia, a curio like Graceland, but with a vintage steam train ride.

I succumb and buy a Christmas ornament with Parton dressed as Santa and eat a chicken salad sandwich served on a butterfly-logo-shaped pretzel. I guess I enjoy Dollywood the way I enjoy going dancing in Berlin gay clubs or karaoke birthday parties: It is an experience, and a fun one, but not what I would choose. I will never, in the vein of a Disney Adult, be a Dolly Adult. More power to those who cherish their season passes. But Parton doesn’t even have to be core to your identity for you to enjoy an intricately branded amusement park. Its unchanging presence is a comfort. If you need to commune with her earthly treasures, there is always Dollywood. May her costumes and wigs remain.

Dollywood will always be a place for fans and dreamers alike to marvel in the wonder of the country icon’s extraordinary career and charming home.

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. That doesn’t mean they compete with premium pairs, but they do give you more to work with than you’d expect for under $35.

These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. Battery life, too, holds up through a full day of use, with a little over seven hours on a single charge and extra top-ups from the case. The sound quality is better than expected for the price, though it leans toward bass-heavy tuning out of the box (you can tweak it in the app, but the app itself is not the most intuitive and takes some getting used to, notes this ZDNET review), and if you’re using a compatible device, LDAC support gives you the option for better audio quality.

There are also a few extras tucked in, like HearID for tuning the sound to your ears and an AI translation feature, though features like that feel more like a bonus than something you will use every day. As for its noise cancellation, it works, but expectations need to stay in check—it reduces steady background noise like engines and traffic, but it won’t match the isolation you get from more expensive earbuds. That lines up with its overall build, as well, which feels a bit basic compared to more expensive options.

Spoilers for Season 3, Episode 1 of Rings of Power are ahead! Read with caution, and watch the show with an Amazon Prime subscription.

As I began my binge of the first four episodes of Rings of Power’s third season, I did not expect to see my favorite dead character return. However, in the first episode of the prequel series to drop on the 2026 TV schedule, a beloved elf made his comeback in a hunting way, and the reason behind why this happened makes the cameo even better.

I’m, of course, talking about the return of Charles Edwards' Celebrimbor. In Season 2, the elven smith was deceived by Sauron, helped the dark lord craft some of the rings, and ultimately died at the hands of the evil being. Then, in Season 3, he appears as a ghost of sorts to talk to Sauron and remind him that he’s not capable of making rings by himself; he’s missing some key information needed to craft them. Speaking to that and how they landed on this big return, co-creator Patrick McKay told me:

So we love the idea that [in] Season 3, Sauron wants to make the One Ring. He wants to be the Dark Lord, but deep down he's insecure. He's worried he can't do it. And for someone as narcissistic and evil as Sauron, that would make him go crazy. He's so angry and defensive, and wants to prove himself so badly. And then we talked about in the writers' room ‘How would we manifest that? What's a way to give you access to what he's feeling?’

That’s how bringing Charles Edwards back as Celebrimbor came about. Before they even finished Season 2, they realized they wanted him to return as a figment of Sauron’s imagination, and the actor was very excited about it, as McKay explained:

And the idea of ‘Well, what if Charles Edwards came back?’ Came along very quickly. I think we spoke to him about it when we were filming the end of Season 2. He loved the idea, and he's really not a ghost. He's the voice in Sauron's head. You know that Sauron feels like he beat him in a way. Celebrimbor, you know, achieved a victory over me that [he] can't surpass.

Now, getting into how this whole sequence was filmed, after McKay told me the reason behind the return, he turned to director Charlotte Brändström and asked why they shot Celebrimbor so simply and “soft in focus.” In response, the director revealed a fascinating line of thinking behind not only that choice, but the decision to make it so Sauron never actually sees Celebrimbor:

I just wanted to be very, very as normal as possible. I didn't want any weird light effects. I didn't want to have only his voice, also because we love him so much, like you. So we wanted to see him and have him be there and have him perform. But I don't want Sauron to see him. So he was always behind Sauron, talking to Sauron. So Sauron never turns around, and if Sauron turns around, then he disappears because obviously he's not there. But it was really, in a way, it's just very, very simple.

Brändström and McKay also explained that when the Orc walks in during the scene and the shot pulls back to Sauron, it was important for Celebrimbor to be gone. That helped signify he wasn’t really there, “he’s just a ghost,” as the director put it. She also explained that this felt like a “real” and “sincere” way to bring Edwards’ elf back. While he could have been translucent like a ghost, or they could have used other techniques to film him, just having him stand behind Sauron and recall what happened between them felt like the best way to do it. And I think they’re right; it really was a haunting sequence.

It also reminded me how much I adore Celebrimbor. While he was deceived by Sauron, he was a genius and a good elf. I miss him dearly, and I was bummed he was gone for good after Season 2. So, to see him come back and explain how Sauron really doesn’t have everything he needs to take over Middle-earth was very satisfying.

Now, to see how Sauron’s mission to forge the One Ring continues, you can stream Episodes 5 and 6 of Rings of Power on Wednesday, November 18, and then you can catch Episodes 7 and 8 – the final two installments of Season 3 – on November 25.

#3671. Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries Face Democratic Leadership Revolt After Midterms

The latest conflict brewing in the Democratic Party’s cold war between the blue dogs and the insurgent progressive wing is the fight over its next congressional leaders. But with no alternate candidates stepping up to run, it’s hard to determine how real the threats to replace Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries actually are.

At least six incoming Democratic senators—including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan, Illinois’s Juliana Stratton, Kansas’s Adam Hamilton, and Maine’s Troy Jackson—have said they won’t support Schumer for majority leader. Michigan senator Elissa Slotkin has called for a “a new generation of leadership.” Even Cory Booker, who praised Schumer for helping engineer last week’s blue wave, stopped short of saying whether he would support him. On Monday, Richard Blumenthal did the same, but walked back his comments later in day, saying he would support Schumer. And Jon Stewart said that the senator “does not understand the urgency of the moment and what the future demands.” Regardless, Schumer is confident. His aides say he has enough votes to become the next majority leader.

In the House, several incoming Democrats—including Claire Valdez, Angela Gonzalez-Torres, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Melat Kiros, Adam Hamawy, Chris Rabb, and Donavan McKinney—have been noncommittal with their support for Jeffries, while Ohio democrat Don Leonard has threatened to seek alternative leadership unless Jeffries changes his position on Israel.

There’s an online effort to prevent Jeffries from becoming Speaker of the House. A change.org petition demanding that House Democrats reject Jeffries as their next Speaker has attracted more than 1 million signatures as of Sunday, with actor Mark Ruffalo among those encouraging people to sign. But scroll to the bottom of the petition, and you’ll find a disclosure: Its creator, Nicole Whitted, is a paid “Change Ambassador” who receives compensation from change.org in connection with the signatures. “Thousands of organizations and brands worldwide run similar programs and in the social-cause space specifically, it’s a way to encourage people with reach and influence to use their voice for causes they care about,” Whitted told Vanity Fair in a statement.

Whitted also said she was traveling to Washington, DC next week to urge congresspeople to vote against Jeffries, and to meet with Representative Ayanna Pressley, whom Whitted told VF she’ll be supporting for Speaker. Pressley’s team did not respond to Vanity Fair’s request for comment sent on Sunday. Neither did her closest congressional allies, Rashida Tlaib, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, or Ilhan Omar.

Reports indicate that some congresspeople have been flooded with calls from constituents urging them to find new party leadership. But one Democratic aide told Vanity Fair that they’ve noticed what they claim is a coordinated effort to undermine Jeffries on social media, including AI-generated videos attacking Jeffries that have gotten tens of thousands of engagements.

The Brooklyn congressman does have good relationships with members of both the moderate “blue dogs” and the party’s progressive flank. Ocasio-Cortez has already backed him, and last month, Representative Ro Khanna declared that “Hakeem Jeffries is going to be Speaker.” “Don’t believe what you’re seeing on the internet,” the aide said. “It’s not reality.”

Schumer’s allies, meanwhile, have been reminding skeptics of the work he did to deliver the Democratic majority. The New York senator helped recruit candidates including Roy Cooper and Sherrod Brown, while the Democratic political operation supporting Senate candidates spent lavishly on competitive races. According to final figures provided to Vanity Fair, Senate Majority PAC and its affiliates spent nearly $407 million across races in eight states, including $150 million in Ohio, $67 million apiece in Iowa and Michigan, $65 million in Maine, and $40 million in Texas, all of which flipped. Another $14 million went toward Kansas, with smaller investments in Mississippi and South Carolina—$2.2 million and $750,000 respectively. Some of that money helped elect candidates who are now skeptical about whether Schumer should stay in charge.

In the House, each party will choose its leadership this month, but in order to become Speaker, a candidate still needs to get a majority of the entire chamber, usually 218 members, to vote for them when the new Congress convenes in January. It’s a little easier in the Senate, where the Democrat will only need to win a simple majority of their own caucus in an anonymous early December vote to become majority leader.

El-Sayed has suggested Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen, although a source close to Van Hollen told Vanity Fair that he isn’t planning to run, instead setting his sights on a potential presidential campaign in 2028. “Prior to selecting a majority leader, Senator Van Hollen believes the caucus needs to have an honest and open conversation about how we move an agenda forward that reflects the will of the American people,” says a Democratic aide familiar with the senator’s thinking. “He’s made clear that Democrats need to use their power to immediately end the illegal war with Iran, advance a robust pro-worker kitchen table agenda, and fight political corruption.”

Another name circulating among Democratic aides is Hawaii senator Brian Schatz, a relatively young progressive who has developed relationships across the party’s ideological factions and is already pursuing the number-two leadership position being vacated by retiring senator Dick Durbin.

“He’s the heir apparent,” one Democratic aide told Vanity Fair, describing Schatz as someone who could appeal to both progressives and moderates. Asked about speculation surrounding his leadership ambitions, Schatz’s spokesperson offered a noncommittal response: “I don’t have anything new to share on this but will keep you posted if that changes.”

Some Democrats are also hesitant to replace their experienced leaders after they’ve been given this narrow opportunity to get stuff done with control of both chambers of Congress. “I don’t think you’d want somebody new who’s, like, learning the ropes while we have the opportunity to really get meaningful legislation passed for the American people,” another Democratic aide said.

Still, the fighting online and on cable news exposes a tension within the Democratic Party. Moderates see the blue wave as vindication of the party’s disciplined, affordability-focused strategy. Progressives see it as a mandate for a more ambitious agenda—and a rejection of the establishment’s familiar faces.

Both factions are claiming the election as their own victory. But before they can fight over what to do with their new power, they’ll have to decide who’s going to lead them.

#3670. Patrick Mahomes and Pregnant Brittany's Comments About Having a Big Family

Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes are preparing for life as a future party of six.

The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback and his wife announced in November 2026 that they are expecting baby No. 4 after Patrick once declared the pair were “done” expanding their family after three kids.

Patrick and Brittany met in high school and began dating in 2012, staying together as Patrick rose through the ranks after being drafted by the Chiefs in 2017. The pair tied the knot in March 2022 in Maui, Hawaii, two years after welcoming daughter Sterling. They later added son Bronze and daughter Golden in 2022 and 2025, respectively.

Keep scrolling to read Patrick and Brittany’s candid quotes about expanding their family:

Patrick and Brittany shared the news that their fourth baby is on the way with a joint Instagram post in November 2026, featuring a beach photo of their eldest three kids gathered around Brittany with their hands on her belly.

“Another blessing from God,” the couple captioned their announcement. “& then there were 6🤍.”

As their post drew plenty of cheers in the comment section, one social media user pointed out that Patrick previously thought three was his limit.

“I thought Patrick said he was done after the last one,” the message read, to which Patrick replied, “ayyy chill chill,” adding three laughing-crying emojis.

The exchange sparked a back-and-forth in the comments, with one fan writing, “People are allowed to change their minds,” and another adding, “Words said by almost every parent.”

Patrick previously declared he was “done” having kids during a July 2024 Kansas City Chiefs training camp press conference, where he stated, “I’m done. I’ll say that. I did three and I’m done.”

“Obviously it’s a blessing to have another baby on the way. I’m excited for it,” Patrick said during a November 11, 2026, press conference, the day after announcing Brittany’s pregnancy. “I’m hoping that me and Bronze can even up the score.”

But while he may have a route he’s aiming for, Patrick noted he would be just as happy with another little girl. As he put it, “I’m just praying for a healthy baby at the end of the day.”

Just days after Brittany gave birth to daughter Golden in January 2025, Patrick Mahomes was already fielding questions about whether another baby was in the cards.

“[I’m] good with three [kids] for right now. My goal was always three, so we’ve had three,” he said in a press conference. “We’ll stick there for a while and see if we need to come back and get another one later on.”

When asked whether a fourth could happen down the line, Patrick didn’t rule it out — saying “maybe” was on the table.

Days later, at another press conference following the Chiefs’ divisional playoff win over the Houston Texans, he joked, “It’s a growing family, but [I] hope we are done growing for a little while.”

Brittany echoed a similar sentiment on a June 2025 episode of the “Whoops” podcast.

“We’re done, we’re done for a while,” she noted. “I don’t know. I mean, I feel like you can never say you’re done. I think three is all I need.”

Patrick has repeatedly spoken about the behind-the-scenes effort required to juggle NFL stardom with family life.

In Netflix’s 2023 Quarterback docuseries, he said, “Everybody sees the game days. They don’t see the day-to-day grind. They don’t see how you have to manage playing football and being a dad and being a husband.”

He continued, “It’s football. You’re gonna have highs. You’re gonna have the lows. You put so much into this that you want to win, you want to succeed. And you want to win that Super Bowl at the end of the year. But I have to be a dad too. I have to be a husband.”

Patrick has also credited growing up in locker rooms — watching his dad, Patrick Mahomes Sr., play baseball — for shaping his desire to start a family young.

#3669. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

#3668. Physint’s ‘Next Cold War,’ OD: Knock’s Scanning Tech, And 8 More Things We Learned At Kojima Productions’ Tokyo Exhibition

Hideo KojimaKojima ProductionsOD: KnockPhysint

When Hideo Kojima rather suddenly left Konami in 2016 and, soon after, opened his own studio, the move sent shockwaves throughout the industry. Today, Kojima Productions has established itself as a AAA development studio within Japan known most of all for 3D-scanning celebrities and developing the Death Stranding franchise, which will soon move beyond gaming as it’s adapted into anime and a live-action film. Looking forward, the studio also plans to expand its range with Physint and OD: Knock in partnership with Xbox.

Itâs one of the more fascinating stories from the last decade of the Japanese games industry, not just for how Kojima Productions came to be but for how it’s sustained itself as a studio. Kojima has leaned on his name recognition to turn the studio into a brand unto itself, and the director keeps himself and the studio in the spotlight through an array of film work, social media posts, radio shows, cameos in TV dramas, and more.

In the upmarket area of Azabudai in central Tokyo, with the historic Tokyo Tower landmark in view, an exhibition looking back on the past decade of the studio has opened for a limited time. Not just chronicling the public history of the studio, the event also featured new information and unseen concept art for Death Stranding, alongside details about the company’s in-development Xbox titles. After visiting the exhibition during its opening days earlier this week, here are ten things we learned about the studio and its array of upcoming titles.

When this exhibition was first announced, Kojima Productions promised not just a look back at the past 10 years of the studio, but a look forward at its in-development work on Physint and OD: Knock as well. That said, actual new information about Physint was light, perhaps as a result of the gameâs turbulent summer which saw publishing shift from Sony to Xbox. All we could gather about work on that game came from some key concepts visible on a display copy of the gameâs script.

Though behind glass, the hefty document made a few significant bits of information aboutÂ Physint visible, providing our first hint about the setting of this new game. Notably, this game will take place within what the script callsÂ  âThe Next Cold War.â This war is defined by three philosophies: HUMINT (“human intelligence”), SIGINT (“signals intelligence,” whatever that may entail, perhaps involving communication in some way), and OSINT (“open-source intelligence”). From this, it seems likely that the term PHYSINT refers to something along the lines of physical intelligence, but thatâs still unconfirmed.

On the scriptâs cover, it appears that there’s a word that comes after Physint and has been redacted, suggesting we don’t yet know the game’s full, final title. We also saw some models of things that appear in-game, including a few mechs that look suspiciously like Metal Gear. Considering Kojima referred to the title as being in the same vein as his earlier stealth series, that’s not entirely unsurprising.

Kojima Productions has become more than a studio: itâs a brand. The merchandise featuring the studioâs logo and spacesuit-wearing Lumens character is proof of this. It appears that having a striking logo was a consideration from early on, as we got a rare look into the design process for the logo and mascot at the show. Notably, while the current logo features a skull inside a spacesuit and emphasizes the head of the character, many of the early designs featured the full character waving a flag. Another shows a knighted character that looks somewhat like Raiden from the Metal Gear series.

While most of the exhibit allowed visitors to freely snap photos of all the concept art and design documents on display, photography was restricted on a short video containing footage of the original prototype for Death Stranding. Luckily, at least part of this video has been shared by Famitsu.

Even in this early state, the game looks rather close to the final release. It seems the concept of running around a sparse, mountainous setting was decided, and we can see rough gameplay of a generic character model picking up cargo and moving around the environment. Another piece of footage shown, taken from further along in development, gives an early glimpse of how BTs were implemented in the game. Theyâre shown acting for more aggressively than they do in the final game, suggesting the emphasis on combat was somewhat toned down before release.

While some concept art for the original Death Stranding has been released to the public via art books, a lot of never-before-seen artwork and footage for the game was shown at the event, making up a sizable portion of the exhibit. This included early attempts at a logo, original sketches by designer Yoji Shinkawa, and more.

Particularly notable, however, were the screens on various walls showing behind-the-scenes footage of motion capture and how the designs for each character changed during development. Early cutscenes were printed on planning documents with Kojimaâs handwritten notes (in amusingly shiny gel pen). And, of course, we got a brief look at the baby doll that was used during these sessions, and the original 3D-printed prototype for the Pods that hold the BBs in the game.

Summaries of documents sent to Sony during the planning stage of Death Stranding to secure support from the company were also on display. These documents explain the concept of “Strand” gameplay as a genre in which multiple players indirectly interact in the same space. The documents also convey that the concept of the game is to âunite us allâ through your actions as you traverse the United States. Early concept art for all of the major characters, including a vastly different version of Fragile, are also on display.

The game’s complex development pipeline was also documented in images that were on display, conveying just how many differing, simultaneous tasks a team must undertake to take a game from concept to finished product within AAA game development.

While some call the first Death Stranding prophetic for how its concepts of connection and delivery were later realized in real life when the world shut down during the Covid-19 pandemic, it turns out Death Stranding 2âs story was radically reworked to consider the altered state of the world as everything shut down to prevent the spread of the virus.

Based on documents shown at the event, the first concept for Death Stranding 2 was produced in 2017, toward the end of development on the first game. Most notable from these documents is a vastly different ending to the game compared to the one we actually gotâa far more optimistic and positive one. The fate of all the characters is revealed, with Fragile alive and leading a delivery team, and Rainy and Tomorrow raising a baby together.

The document also details subterranean gameplay that would allow for greater variety in traversal, though the overall concept of connecting the world was present from this early state. It also appears that even at this time, Elle Fanning had already been considered for Tomorrow, as her name is brought up in the document.

We will be exhibiting âMADO,â a telepresence system that enables seamless two-way communication between remote locations. We used it during the COVID-19 pandemic for performance capture sessions connecting Los Angeles and Tokyo. Throughout the exhibition, âMADOâ will continuouslyâ¦ https://t.co/Y7Jc3HzYJG pic.twitter.com/oxwhnpvQGS

— HIDEO_KOJIMA (@HIDEO_KOJIMA_EN) October 18, 2026

To aid in development, and especially with scanning actors and conducting motion capture when borders were closed during the pandemic, Kojima Productions developed its own communication system to aid in networking with actors and remote workers, known as Mado (Japanese for âwindowâ). Developed by MUSVI Corporation, Mado was used to connect people in a more immersive manner than a mere video call could allow for. Kojima Productions used it to connect with motion capture studios in Los Angeles for more effective direction of actors during these sessions, even when separated across different countries and time zones.

For the exhibition, the technology was on display with a direct feed to the Kojima Productions office in real time, providing a so-called window into the studio. During our visit, this showed the area in the studio where 3D scans of actors are done, but it seems that this will be changed up throughout the event.

ãããªæãã§éº»å¸å°ãã«ãºã®ã£ã©ãªã¼ã®ãçªãðªã¨ã³ã¸ãã­ã®ãçªãðªãç¹ãã§ãã¾ãããã¾ã«å°å³¶ç£ç£ãç»å ´ãã¦ãã¾ãï¼#ã³ã¸ãã­å±ã#BeyondtheStrand https://t.co/ECvNIsSaP1 pic.twitter.com/LuChYDrz09

— Ayako (Touchy!) (@Kaizerkunkun) November 5, 2026

Staff members at Kojima Productions will make unscheduled appearances on the video conferencing tool to speak with attendees throughout the duration of the exhibition. During our visit, Kojima himself made a brief appearance to speak with visitors in Japanese and English. Donât take that as a guarantee that visiting the event will be a chance to talk to the man himself, but itâs seemingly not impossible.

Kojima Productions is far more than just the games it develops. To an extent, the exhibit feels as much like a showcase for the studio’s multimedia and merchandising efforts as it does a window into the company’s game development process. An entire section of the exhibition floor is dedicated to the various external partnerships the studio has created, including storyboards for its various anime projects including Death Stranding Isolations, and even credit cards released in collaboration with Japanese bank MUFG.

These partnerships were peppered all around the show floor. In the photography-prohibited showcase of new information for OD: Knock, a special RIMOWA custom suitcase to hold a statue of the gameâs protagonist was on display. The case included the letters H K on a luggage tag, surrounded by crows. Another section featured the many musical partnerships for Death Stranding 1 and 2. Expanding Kojima Productions beyond gaming was a key point of emphasis throughout the exhibitâthe merchandise store at the event includes new clothing collaborations with F.C. Real Bristol and a chibi-fied plushie of Kojima himself.

Attendees of the exhibition get a chance to play an early demo of a planned AR game for mobile phones created in partnership with Niantic Spatial. Called Death Stranding: Odradek (Tokyo Prototype), it uses the technology underpinning PokÃ©mon Go to have you deliver parcels in the real world. Currently this is very scripted (the only available deliveries exist within the Azabudai area of Tokyo surrounding the exhibit), but one can assume the game could automatically generate new deliveries for players anywhere in the world in a potential future version for general audiences.

Players would also need to care for their own BB, and the game uses the camera on your phone to scan the world around you for signposts and guidance from other players. Taking the Strand gameplay concept into this new title, players can âlikeâ helpful guidance, and it’s even possible to run into BTs when using your phone’s camera to look around the world.

New information about the upcoming horror game OD: Knock was showcased at the exhibition, although photography was strictly prohibited. However, what we saw was a game taking clear cues from the experiments Kojima did with PT and continuing his attempts to bring the worlds of live-action filmmaking and video games together.

In order to model how traversal is presented in the game, Kojima and his team recorded a walkthrough of a real-world environment using a first-person perspective captured on GoPro cameras, before recreating the fisheye perspective and framing of these shots virtually within the gameâs engine. One comparison image showed a photograph of a dual-GoPro image depicting a dirty kitchen countertop and a window looking out onto a damp British street, compared to a similar shot captured in-engine.

Clearly not content with only scanning people for his games, Kojima has taken things further when it comes to what he will digitize. Detailing the 3D scanning process, the exhibition confirmed that the team partnered with 2024 TBS TV drama Sayonara, Maestro! in order to capture detailed 3D scans of many of the show’s sets for reuse in the game.

The drama, which follows a conductor named Natsume (played by Drive My Car actor Hidetoshi Nishijima) returning to Japan and attempting to rebuild his relationship with his daughter, could not be further from the horror story being presented in OD. However, the show makes use of sets for the interior of the home the pair live in. The Kojima Productions team took detailed scans of the sets to help them model a family home, though just how that setting will be used in the game has not yet been revealed. Kojima’s radio program is also produced in partnership with TBS, likely helping to facilitate the director’s efforts to scan the set.

Similarly, the team has digitized a number of pieces of vintage furniture, such as old dressers, in order to ensure that such furniture in-game looked sufficiently aged.

The Kojima Productions exhibition in Tokyo runs until December 20th, and fans of the studioâs games are sure to enjoy the hundreds of unseen pieces of concept art and design documents that provide a window into the past decade of game development at the studio. More than that, however, it shows how expansive the Kojima Productions mission has become. If Kojimaâs work at Konami was largely restricted to his work on Metal Gear Solid and his activities as a game developer, Kojima Productions has made him the head of an entertainment company and brand that happens to make games.

The fact the company has organized its own exhibition where movies and merchandise are as prominent as game design is proof of that. The RIMOWA custom case? Kojima showcased his own suitcase in a separate exhibition last month in Tokyo. He’s worked with Prada. The company routinely works with celebrities known for acting and filmmaking, and as you enter the exhibit, thank-you messages from many such figures including Norman Reedus and Mamoru Oshii welcome you to the event.

This isnât a bad thing. Itâs just emblematic of how, as game development becomes more expensive, supporting such high-budget work requires that you produce more than just a single game or DLC at the end of the road. You must produce a high-quality game, of course, and the concept art and design documents showing just how much effort the studio puts into its games prove that Kojima Productions takes that very seriously. But creating passion that will have fans flocking to buy that expensive jacket with the studio logo on it and charge it to a branded credit card? Thatâs something else entirely.

#3667. Val Chmerkovskiy’s Son Gives Him Advice After Shocking 'DWTS' Elimination

Val Chmerkovskiy is finding solace in his 3-year-old son, Rome, after his shocking Dancing With The Stars elimination during Grammy Night.

“It’s OK to lose right?” Chmerkovskiy, 40, asked Rome in a Thursday, November 11, social media video.

Rome, whom the three-time mirrorball champ shares with fellow DWTS pro Jenna Johnson, was merely proud that his dad gave it his all on the dance floor.

“Yeah, you try your best,” Rome adorably replied. “If you don’t win [some] times, you try to do it so many times.”

Chmerkovskiy further acknowledged that it’s important to “learn how to do both,” meaning winning and losing.

“It’s OK to be sad when you lose for a little bit,” the dance pro acknowledged.

Despite two impressive performances during the Tuesday, November 10, live show, Chmerkovskiy and celebrity partner Jenna Dewan were eliminated just shy of the show’s coveted semifinals. (Johnson, 32, and her partner, Harry Shum Jr., are still in the competition.)

“People want you to win because you’re a great dancer,” Rome added. “[Whether] you win or you lose, you try again on a different day. If you wanna win, you need to move your body and do it so fast and then you win. You get the champion[ship].”

While Chmerkovskiy admittedly felt disheartened to have walked away from DWTS season 35 empty-handed, he felt “better” after speaking with Rome.

“I have you in my life,” Chmerkovskiy noted, before Rome added that he will “always” be his dad’s “friend.”

“You’re not my friend, you’re my son, which I love so much,” Chmerkovskiy clarified. “We’re also buds, right? … What did we learn about winning and losing?”

Rome further revealed that he discovered the importance of competitions is that “friends make you happy.”

“Friends make us happy, and that it’s OK to lose,” Chmerkovskiy explained. “As long as you try.”

Rome repeated, “As long as you try. I love you so much.”

Neither Chmerkovskiy nor Dewan, 45, harbor any grudges in the midst of their early departure from the ballroom competition.

“Every week is a shocker,” Chmerkovskiy, who also faced a one-week suspension earlier this season for making a controversial comment about judge Carrie Ann Inaba, told Extra on Tuesday. “It’s very competitive. A lot of great couples out there. Wishing everybody the best, and I’m gonna be rooting from home. I thought we had a great season.”

Chmerkovskiy and Dewan had been early frontrunners in the competition, which often sparked fan criticism of the Rookie actress’ prior dance experience.

“I keep saying that I knew it would be hard. I knew that would be a physically challenging situation. I didn’t realize how emotionally and mentally tough the whole process is too,” Dewan previously told Us last month. “It’s a good tough. That’s why you feel so alive while doing this. It’s all the good things, but with that comes all the colors. All the shades.”

Dancing With the Stars airs Tuesdays on ABC and Disney+ at 8 p.m. ET.
