#3666. Elon Musk’s Cybertruck Is Dumb, Ugly, and Mercifully Dead

In March 2024, a Tesla Cybertruck speeding down Sunset Boulevard slammed head-on into the Beverly Hills Hotel’s iconic entrance sign just before midnight. Passersby winding through the Flats slowed down to watch as Elon Musk’s statue to his own insecurities—the stainless steel embodiment of nuance-free American ego—demolished in front of Hollywood’s unofficial canteen.

Every decade gets the iconography it deserves. At just about the midpoint of the 2020s, ours had arrived, fully formed.

And now the Cybertruck is dead, which is wonderful news. Musk, who’s having a historically bad November, announced late last week that Tesla will be “winding down” production of the Cybertruck around mid-2027, putting an end to the most hated car in America. I was going to call it the most polarizing car in America, but honestly, no one likes this thing. And it’s not entirely due to anti-Elon sentiment: Tesla’s general sales have been relatively steady, going down a bit as Musk went full DOGE mode in 2025 before rebounding in 2026. People like Elon’s cars. They just do not like the Cybertruck.

True, its death has been mourned by some—especially the self-selecting devotees who installed bulletproof glass in their Cybertrucks before shooting them with rifles. These people exist. But mostly, the news has been greeted with a rush of enthusiasm, relief, and, more than anything else, blue-pilled schadenfreude.

Now would be the right moment in the news cycle for an art writer such as myself to make a contrarian argument: that the Cybertruck was secretly a design masterpiece—some kind of neo-Donald Judd breakthrough unleashed ahead of its time.

I am not going to make that argument, because that is not true. Not even close. No one in the future will look back on the Cybertruck as an unheralded art object. It’s The Jetsons for meatheads, a Batmobile for people who secretly root for the Joker. It looks like a birdhouse designed by Zaha Hadid, which I would love to have as a vessel for feeding hungry birds at my (sadly hypothetical) Zaha Hadid house. But I would not want it as a vehicle to park in a driveway. It is a bad car.

And yet, that crashed Cybertruck in front of the Beverly Hills Hotel is seared into my brain, playing on repeat like the most un-subtle Lana Del Rey song ever written. Even beyond that crash, the Cybertruck is the ultimate symbol of this surreal and cruel decade, one that started with a global pandemic and a government suggesting the possibility of a bleach injection as treatment. It’s a decade that wound through four years of a former president denying the lawful election of a current president, only to see that former president return to power. Through it all, we’ve sunk deeper into our collective psychosis—one that’s forced us into rooms with our devices, addicted to social media and artificial intelligence, consuming half-real information and spewing it back out into the world.

It’s a perfect world for the Tesla Cybertruck to define.

The Cybertruck arrived right at the dawn of the decade, in what we can now see as a completely different timeline.

Musk unveiled the car in November 2019 at Tesla’s design studio. Head designer Franz von Holzhausen attempted to demonstrate the vehicle’s shatterproof glass by hurtling a metal ball at a window at full speed. The window shattered. Great omen! It was also pretty weird that Musk was introduced by a hologram of someone called “Cybergirl,” who people speculated was actually a hologram of Grimes, the pop star Musk was dating at the time.

Plenty of design press fawned over the shiny new thing—“Long live the Cybertruck. See you in the Thunderdome,” wrote Dwell. But Wired wisely asked the opinion of an actual expert: Raphael Zammit, who chairs automobile design at Motor City’s own College for Creative Studies.

“I was like, ‘Oh my goodness! What did Tesla do? What did they do?” he said. “It literally breaks every rule we tell to our students. It’s what we tell them not to do.”

Regardless, the Cybertruck started to infiltrate the cultural atmosphere. It was lampooned on The Simpsons. There were countless memes. It was embraced, very early, by rappers. Weeks after the unveiling, Travis Scott used his personal connections to the Tesla CEO (they did Christmas together with the Kardashian-Jenners) to snag a Cybertruck for his video for “Gang Gang,” a posse cut with the Cactus Jack crew.

Three years later, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, and Tyler, the Creator featured the Cybertruck in their video for “Cash In, Cash Out”—rendered in Claymation. Offset’s video for “Swing My Way” has Anok Yai sitting atop a Cybertruck. Bad Bunny said, “Me monté en la Cybertruck y me acordé de la Montero de los viejos tiempo.” Meek Mill said, “They was doing cyber attacks, so I bought a Cybertruck.”

The cars fascinated artists too. Julia Wachtel’s CyberChrist, on view at Todd Von Ammon’s DC gallery, von ammon co, earlier this year, pictures Jesus Christ pulling an elongated Cybertruck behind him. I recall with great happiness the perverse thrill of Frieda Toranzo Jaeger’s Cybertruck, a painting in her 2022 show at MoMA PS1. These artists were certainly taking a critical eye toward the Cybertruck, but for some art collectors, there was nothing ironic about it. At least, a specific kind of collector. When I arrived at the convention center for Art Basel Miami Beach in 2024, the first full year of Cybertruck distribution, there was a line of Cybertrucks wrapped around the block.

But that’s the thing about the Cybertruck: There was always more supply than demand. Musk initially hoped to sell 250,000 units per year. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, Tesla moved nearly 39,000 of them in 2024, a decent start. In 2025, sales dropped, then dropped again in 2026.

Perhaps the Cybertruck could have endured the ridicule of design experts, car enthusiasts, and aesthetes with even just a whiff of good taste if it weren’t for the massive backlash that accompanied Musk’s move into radical right-wing politics, and his full-throated support of Donald Trump. After his efforts at DOGE resulted in the gutting of USAID and other agencies, along with unprecedented and remorseless mass firings, Cybertrucks started getting vandalized around the country. Some owners tried to protect their weird boxy investments with mea culpa stickers—“I bought this before Elon went crazy,” etc.—but no one believed that, or really cared. The cars got defaced. No one stepped in to intervene. The Cybertrucks deserved it.

There was also a bleaker incident that parallels the Cybertruck at the Beverly Hills Hotel: the dystopian hellscape of the Cybertruck that exploded on the Las Vegas Strip, in front of the Trump International Hotel & Casino. The man responsible for that explosion served in the US Army, and authorities believe he suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound just before the vehicle detonated. The Beverly Hills crash was an accident in which no one was harmed—but the charred, deadly remains of the truck in Las Vegas seemed downright terrifying, a vision of American capitalism and greed that had met its grisly moment.

Perhaps now, with a new era of Washington poised to define the final years of this most delirious of decades, we’ll eventually look back at the Cybertruck with at least some nostalgia for its silliness, its boxy stupidity, its pop culture ubiquity. If it does linger in the annals of history, maybe we’ll think of the Cybertruck as a roadbound folly of the world’s first trillionaire, and a footnote in Musk’s legacy, for better or for worse.

Put it this way: By the time Hollywood studio heads arrived at the Polo Lounge for their Monday power lunches, the mess of the Cybertruck that had crashed at the Beverly Hills Hotel the night before was gone. Almost as if it never happened at all.

It's been a wild week for fans of the superhero genre, especially folks who have been watching the DC movies in order. The internet exploded when it was revealed that James Gunn was stepping away at co-CEO of DC Studios, with the public left wondering if we'll ever see his first phase of announced projects called Gods and Monsters. There's been a ton of discourse online, although I think the issue with the DC TV shows (which are streaming with a HBO Max subscription) have the same issue as some Netflix series.

Gunn's DCU might be cooked, and there are countless questions about upcoming DC movies and TV shows. Variety wrote a long story about what's reportedly happening behind the scenes, as well as the perceived missteps of the shared universe. Regarding what happened on the small screen, the publication blamed the three-year wait between seasons of Peacemaker for the sophomore entry being less popular than the first.

I personally loved how Peacemaker Season 2 retconned the Justice League and helped establish the new DCU, but not everyone was quite as invested as me. Fans have bee wondering if Peacemaker might get a Season 3, although that seems more unlikely with Gunn out.

While all eyes are on what DC did or didn't do wrong, I think that this symptom is something that's also happened for plenty of shows that are available with a Netflix subscription. We've seen a number of years pass between season of Stranger Things, Wednesday, Squid Games and more. While those are some of the streaming service's most popular projects, there are fans who dropped off or lost interest due to the long gap between seasons. Considering how many TV shows many of us watch, those years result in fans not really remembering what had happened during previous seasons.

Netflix also has a penchant for cancelling shows after just one season, and that very well might be happening at DC as well. Fans have been wondering if we'll get Lanterns Season 2, and concerns over the show's future have only gotten louder now that James Gunn and Peter Safran are out. Creature Commandos also hit HBO back in 2024, and there's been no indication that the animated series will get another batch of episodes. While folks are dissecting ever decision the Guardians of the Galaxy filmmaker made as co-CEO of DC Studios, I can't help but notice connective tissue with some problems that have followed Netflix.

Only time will tell what Gunn's replacement Former Marvel Studios executive and producer Jeremy Latcham is cooking up at DC. Fans are nervous about what's coming next, especially since we're still so early into the run of the DCU.

The next DC movie hitting theaters on Man of Tomorrow, directed by Gunn and releasing on July 9, 2027. What comes next for the shared universe after that sequel's release is anyone's guess.

For now, itâs recommended to remove any payment information saved to your Humble account in case of unauthorized access, at least until these issues are resolved. #3661. Avedon Director Ron Howard On Richard Avedon’s “Creative Courage,” and His Favorite Images From 'In the American West'

In his new documentary Avedon, director Ron Howard traces the vivid legacy of the influential photographer Richard Avedon, which premieres November 11 on Netflix. “The subjects he worked with on the commercial side of his career were dazzling and beautiful, and he was so entertaining and expressive in the way that he would shoot them. But I really had no idea how he applied his status, his influence, his access to tell this other kind of story about human beings that was honest, insightful, and more journalistic,” Howard tells Vanity Fair.

The glamorous heights of Avedon’s career were what first caught Howard’s attention. “I became aware of him really in the ’80s. Then it was even his TV commercials, like Brooke Shields [in Calvin Klein ads],” Howard said. Later, he realized a few of his favorite portraits were taken by Avedon. One of these was a portrait of a young Kareem Abdul-Jabbar at a playground in New York holding a basketball “and kind of casually standing there looking straight into the camera. It’s not against a white background…” notes Howard. “I know Kareem a little bit. It so captured the foundational strength of character and intelligence that Kareem carried with him along with his basketball talent.”

Initially, Howard, who spent three years making the film, thought it was going to be more focused on the fashion and celebrity worlds that Avedon inhabited. However, his fascination with photographs like “sad Marilyn” (Avedon’s 1957 portrait of Marilyn Monroe) grew into a respect for the full breadth of Avedon’s career, and his “creative courage as an artist.”

In the film, footage of Avedon and new interviews with Lauren Hutton, Tina Brown, Adam Gopnik, Hilton Als, Joel Meyerowitz, Larry Gagosian, and Avedon’s son John, among others, paint a picture of a driven, curious, and sometimes mercurial artist. In the 1950s, Avedon’s career took off when he began shooting for Harper’s Bazaar, Vogue, and Vanity Fair. He injected a sense of play and prewar European glamour into his images by drawing inspiration from the films of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers. Eventually, he ventured into documentary assignments and more political subjects, including Nothing Personal (1964), a photobook with text by James Baldwin that captured the tensions of the Civil Rights era alongside a broader look at American life, a three panel portrait of anti-war protesters the Chicago Seven, and members of America’s political and financial elite at the time of the country’s bicentennial (“The Family”) for Rolling Stone. At the height of his career, he seemingly shifted quite easily from photographing celebrities to documenting anti-war protests and the counterculture of the 1960s, even when his work was met with mixed reactions.

Dovima with elephants, evening dress by Dior, Cirque d’Hiver, Paris, August 1955.

James Baldwin, New York, January 9, 1963.

Avedon (left) with Gloria Vanderbilt and Sidney Lumet at a party for the movie premiere of East of Eden (dir. Elia Kazan), 1955.

“We tried to reflect the risks he took and the transitions he made with his art and his career,” Howard shares. Had Howard made the documentary in Avedon’s lifetime, he would have liked to have asked him directly about the turning points in his career. “In all the interviews, he just kind of made it seem like it was a natural step. But to me, it's not a natural step to stop getting thousands and thousands of dollars an hour to shoot commercials and shoot for the world's most read magazines, and go to Vietnam where no one was really. He wasn’t on assignment initially… he just committed.”

In 1979, the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth, Texas, commissioned Avedon to capture a portrait of the West. He worked on this ambitious portfolio periodically through 1984, traveling across 17 states like California, Colorado, Iowa, North Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming, with assistants and a researcher, Laura Wilson, who helped Avedon arrange 752 portrait sittings. (Wilson also documented the making of the project in her own remarkable photographs and writing.) In total, Avedon printed 124 photographs (some as large as four feet tall) and exhibited them at the museum in 1985. The result was In the American West—a turning point in Avedon’s career. Prior to the project’s completion, in 1983, Vanity Fair ran five photographs from the eventual series, showing coal miners covered in dust and one lone oil worker alongside a feature on Wagner’s operas and an excerpt of Gabriel García Márquez’s Chronicle of a Death Foretold.

“One of the reasons I was drawn to [In the American West] is because my family roots are in the Midwest,” Howard says. “I see a lot of truth in these images.”

Avedon conducting a portrait session for In the American West beside his 8x10 camera.

In a similar fashion to August Sander’s massive undertaking People of the 20th Century, Avedon went looking for “men and women who work at hard, uncelebrated jobs, the people who are often ignored or overlooked,” Wilson wrote. In doing so he joined a whole legion of photographers whose images have come to define broad swaths of middle and western America. But unlike common readings of Sander’s project at the time, Avedon was clear that his version of the West was totally subjective, more of a cinematic panorama than an objective record. He was emphatic that all photographs are filtered through the photographer’s eye, and become their interpretation. Through Wilson, he declared, “This is a fictional West. I don’t think the West of these portraits is any more conclusive than the West of John Wayne.”

Below, Howard reflects on five of his favorite photographs from Avedon’s In the American West.

“I asked if that was makeup, and I was assured that none of it was. [Avedon] set up, and just as workers were coming off their shift, he was getting them in front of the camera. I mean, wow, this is what these workers look like. This is what was in their lungs and their pores. I have cousins and uncles who worked in the oil fields. I never had any idea that they had their days looking like they’d been through what this guy has been through on his shift.”

“The boy with the rattlesnake was the first photo that [Avedon] took where he knew he was going to get at something deeper... He felt like this was almost religious iconography in a way, or mythic. [The subject] was a teenager. As Avedon says, he's a boy turning into a man, and here he's doing this kind of work, so it speaks to a transformation. It also speaks of that region as a very pragmatic region. My own dad, to try to get some spending money [in the ’30s], was hunting and trapping raccoons to sell skins to the junk dealer or possums they could eat. Absolutely just a pragmatic way of life there. So that image always resonated with me. It is also featured in the documentary because it was the proof in [Avedon’s] mind that he was going to be able to identify moments and individuals that would be arresting and mean a lot on an artistic level.”

“The beekeeper is, of course, a stunning image–one that doesn't have that much to do with the American West. I think [Avedon] could have found somebody like that in almost any corner of the planet, but it certainly is fascinating and a tribute to the research team that was working with him to help find him.”

“The maintenance worker who’s dressed up in a really flashy suit, suit jacket, tie and hat, that just looks very familiar to me. I mean, the jacket and all the embroidery on it, the flowers, I never saw anything like that with my family. They didn’t have that kind of flourish. This guy looks like he could be a country western singer or could be trying to be a country western star. But the hat, the tie, the gaze, the posture looks very, very familiar to me. That looks like a hardworking guy getting dressed up on the weekend.”

#3660. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3658. 'General Hospital' Star Randall England Dead at 75 After Cancer Battle

General Hospital alum Randall England has died after a battle with esophageal cancer. He was 75.

“Of all his roles, being a father and ‘Pappaw’ to his grandchildren meant the most to him,” England’s family wrote in an obituary shared on Wednesday, November 11.

The soap star, widely known for his captivating portrayal of Jack Slater in the ABC daytime drama, died on September 25 while surrounded by loved ones in Los Angeles, California.

England played the villainous character during an eight-month run on GH from 1984 to 1985. His character Jack claimed to be a flourishing film producer upon his arrival in Port Charles, but it’s later revealed that he’s actually a jewel thief.

The obituary noted that England was an “accomplished baseball and football player” before he made a name for himself in Hollywood.

“A fateful trip to New York City changed the course of his life,” per the obit, which stated that England dabbled in modeling and traveled the world, touching down in London, Zurich and Milan. He expanded his résumé with advertising and commercial work over the years, ranging from campaigns with Viceroy cigarettes, Dunlop tires, Michelob and PlayStation.

After a successful audition landed him a role in Los Angeles, the actor finally found the place he’d eventually call homee. Randall planted roots in Beverly Hills and remained there for 40 years.

He tied the knot with Jennifer Leigh Herreras in 1987. Two years later, the couple welcomed a daughter, Micaela Rae, in 1989.

Throughout his career, he secured many notable film rules. England was cast in Beverly Hills Chihuahua, Hellborn, Skyscraper, Dream Machine and Shiner.

He also secured TV roles on The Young and the Restless and Baywatch. Fans even recognize the actor from his music video cameo for Maroon 5’s “Sugar.”

Described as someone who was “charming, loving, and generous with his time and energy,” his loved ones said that “Randall was someone people could count on.”

“Friends, family, and former students have remembered his authenticity and the steady presence he offered in their lives,” the obituary continued. “He offered encouragement and advice freely. His legacy lives on in the people he loved, taught and supported.”

In the wake of his death, England’s family has asked that memorial donations be made to the Esophageal Cancer Action Network.

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

While Kylie Jenner continues to make headlines for her glittery ensembles and ties to Y2K trends, she’s also been drawn attention due to several legal situations. Now, amid the ongoing situations, Jenner’s legal representative is speaking out.

The latest suit to be filed against Jenner came from a former housekeeper, Dinora Carolina Cabria Amaya. In her suit, which was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on November 5, Amaya – who reportedly began working for Jenner in March 2025, claimed she was regularly denied overtime payment and worked long hours along with purportedly not having her travel costs covered for traveling between the cosmetics mogul’s properties. Per Amaya, she earned $40 an hour while working six days a week.

Amaya also alleged that she was bitten by a dog while cleaning one of the doghouses on one of the Kardashian family member’s properties. Michael Rhodes, Jenner’s legal rep, released a statement to Page Six, in which he took issue with this latest suit as well as the other filings:

These latest cases are being brought by the same lawyer who previously filed claims on behalf of Kylie’s former household staff. It’s clear that this lawyer wants to use publicity to try and extract an unwarranted payday.

After Birkin Backlash, Kylie Jenner Explained Why She Has So Many Of The Pricey Bags

Amaya, who was allegedly fired in February 2026 is reportedly suing Jenner for disability discrimination, wrongful termination and retaliation among other alleged offenses. The first suit filed against Jenner (who’s also been handling real estate matters as of late) in 2026 was filed by her former housekeeper, Angelica Hernandez Vasquez, in April, and she accused Jenner of harassing and discriminating against her due to her immigration status and religious faith and made other claims as well.

Another former housekeeper, Juana Delgado Soto, filed suit against Jenner and her brands two weeks later and accused them of discrimination, retaliation and harassment. And, this past June, a Jane Doe – who was reportedly a private chef – filed suit against Jenner and others for purported pregnancy discrimination and wrongful termination.

Those various cases are currently at different stages of the legal process and, at this point, Kylie Jenner has denied wrongdoing via her legal teams. As part of his recent statement, Rhodes also had this to say about the cases:

We’re not going to be intimidated into doing that. As such, we’ll defend these meritless cases vigorously and look forward to telling our side of the story.

Ahead of this series of lawsuits, Kylie Jenner has been embroiled in other legal matters over the years. Reports swirled around Jenner in 2020 after it was alleged that she used forged tax documents to overstate her wealth. She was also involved in a few disputes in 2017 regarding trademarks and logos.

When it comes to the case involving Dinora Carolina Cabria Amaya, it remains to be seen whether it’ll develop any further. #3655. Exclusive: See Camila Morrone in Netflix’s Sexually Charged ‘The Age of Innocence’

When Edith Wharton was in her mid-40s, she had a sexual awakening. For decades, the celebrated novelist had been stuck in a dull, loveless marriage to Edward Robbins Wharton, a fellow patrician 12 years older than her. Then she met debonair journalist William Morton Fullerton and fell—hard.

“I have drunk of the wine of life at last,” she wrote on May 21, 1908, in the document Wharton scholars call her “love diary.” “I have known the thing best worth knowing, I have been warmed through & through, never to grow quite cold again til the end.” Years later, she’d finally divorce Teddy and move abroad, where she’d channel these transformative experiences into her most celebrated novel: The Age of Innocence, published in 1920.

“I was at a place where I said I want to do anything except period, because I’ve done so much period,” says showrunner Emma Frost, whose résumé includes a trio of lavish historical series: The White Queen, The White Princess, and The Spanish Princess. But when Netflix asked if she might be interested in adapting The Age of Innocence, she reconsidered. Frost had read the novel and seen Martin Scorsese’s lush 1993 adaptation, starring Daniel Day-Lewis, Winona Ryder, and Michelle Pfeiffer. “I remembered it was the very first love story I ever engaged with that felt truly adult,” she says.

Then she learned that Wharton had actually written two alternate endings to her book—“and both the alternative endings have explicit sexual content.” It was a surprising development considering the published version of the novel, which is full of tortured yearning—there’s an achingly erotic moment concentrated on a character silently lifting a velvet ribbon to his lips—but contains no actual sex.

Her discovery led Frost to fall down a Whartonian rabbit hole. She learned everything about Wharton’s life-changing affair, devouring the 300 love letters the author had sent to Fullerton. “Once you actually delve into the Wharton archive, there’s all sorts of unpublished works that are explicitly about this experience of being a very sexual woman,” Frost says.

“The yearning, and the tension, and the longing, and the looks, and all of that delicious stuff is so important. I’ve been really obsessive in trying to capture that, and be very faithful to it.” But the sexy stuff in Wharton’s archive is what inspired Frost to make an Age of Innocence that’s not so innocent after all.

Ben Radcliffe as Newland Archer, Kristine Froseth as May Welland, and Camila Morrone as Ellen Olenska

As in the novel, her series—premiering on Netflix February 18—follows Gilded Age aristocrat Newland Archer, a gentleman lawyer preparing for a staid but satisfying life with his betrothed, well-bred ingenue May Welland. But his carefully planned future is thrown into disarray when May’s cousin, the independent-minded Countess Ellen Olenska, arrives in New York under a cloud of scandal, and with a highly unusual desire for this era: She wants to divorce her horrible husband.

Unlike the novel, Frost’s version also has nudity and graphic content: masturbation, voyeurism, a narratively important threesome. It’s not your grandmother’s Edith Wharton. But Frost would argue it’s very true to the spirit of its author.

And there’s more to her Age of Innocence than sex, of course. Wharton’s novel is told from Newland’s limited perspective; we only know what he knows, and see what he sees. Frost, though, wanted to make her version a true three-hander. “I think when you stay just with the male point of view, May becomes the antagonist, and Ellen becomes the thing to be won or saved or rescued. And that wasn’t something I wanted to do,” she says. “I wanted to have these two women really existing as flesh-and-blood women who we can care about.”

To accomplish this, she’d need a dynamic cast featuring The Witcher alum Ben Radcliffe as Newland, Kristine Froseth—who also stars in the Wharton-based Apple series The Buccaneers—as May, and Emmy nominee Camila Morrone as Ellen. Newland, says Frost, “doesn’t fit in with this society. He’s straining at the conventions. Ellen represents that other world, greater freedom”—the very freedom Wharton herself found when she ditched both New York City and her husband.

Radcliffe seemed to understand his character on a profound level. “There was a stillness that nobody else brought, and you could just see everything happening behind his eyes,” Frost says. Morrone, best known for playing a May Welland-esque character on Prime Video’s Daisy Jones and the Six, was similarly well-suited for hers: “She’s the most fearless actor I have ever met.”

Kristine Froseth as May Welland and Camila Morrone as Ellen Olenska

And then there’s May, who might be the trickiest member of the trio for modern audiences to understand. Unlike her fiancé and her cousin, she likes occupying a prescribed role in buttoned-up 1870s society—and she’ll do what she must to protect her perch, without malice or cruelty. Froseth found a way to convey the character’s depth and dimensionality.

“I always felt quite indignant on May’s behalf. All she ever did was fall in love with a man who courts her, say yes to a man who proposes to her, do everything right—and then along comes her cousin, and suddenly her choices are be shamed, be dumped, or fight for him,” says Frost. “Kristine just brings this light into the room. You love her, and you want her to be happy, and not to be disappointed. And that was the essential quality for me with May.”

There’s no real antagonist in Frost’s Age of Innocence. “I think it felt complex and morally right to keep saying, ‘There’s three people here that have feelings. What is the right thing in this situation?’” she says.

Kristine Froseth as May Welland and Ben Radcliffe as Newland Archer

Frost also wanted to flesh out the world of Wharton’s novel by adding mentions and subplots about real-world events its characters may have been aware of—like the Comstock Act of 1873, an anti-obscenity law that has never been repealed—and by introducing new settings like a boxing gym, where Newland goes to work out his aggression. In the series, that’s also where he befriends journalist Ned Winsett, a character from Wharton’s book reimagined here as a Black New Yorker played by Kel Matsena. “For me, it felt like a very organic thing to have non-white characters” in the series, says Frost. “They are the new ideas. They are the exciting conversations. They are the music that’s coming in.” Casting Argentine-American Morrone as the Countess Olenska, “making Ellen part of that influx, [also] felt right.”

As in any good period piece, the show’s costumes—designed by Daniel Orlandi, whom Frost calls a “bona fide genius”—and production design, overseen by Jean-François Campeau, are vital storytelling engines as well. “We always talked about these ridiculous little Victorians, trying so hard to believe they could live from the neck upwards—somehow divorce themselves from their animal nature and their bodies. The clothes and the sets were all part of that,” says Frost. “Weather and animals are really big motifs in the show. It’s about contrasting these people with the real, natural world and the weather that kind of goes, ‘Ha, ha, ha, you think you can somehow exist away from nature?’”

Camila Morrone as Ellen Olenska and Ben Radcliffe as Newland Archer

Though Frost and her team paid careful attention to detail, she cautions that sticklers may find things to quibble about if they examine the costumes carefully: “Our bustles are slightly smaller than they should be in the period.” And that’s without even considering the sexual aspect of the series. “Oh, there will be some pearl clutching,” Frost laughs. “Totally, I’m sure.”

But an expert in period drama like Frost knows when embracing historical accuracy actually matters, and when to let it slide. Wharton did too. While writing The Age of Innocence, Frost says, the author discovered that famed Swedish soprano Christina Nilsson did not actually sing Faust in New York in the year she'd set her novel—even though a performance of Faust starring Nilsson was the catalyst for her book’s action. Wharton wrestled with whether she should include the scene anyway. “And then she wrote to her sister-in-law and said, ‘I don’t care. Atmosphere is more important than historical accuracy.’”

“So I’m like, ‘Okay, Edith. If it’s good enough for you, it is good enough for me.’”

#3653. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3652. Patrick Mahomes Reveals What He Hopes 4th Baby's Sex Will Be Amid Pregnancy

Patrick Mahomes is ready to add to his family’s roster amid wife Brittany Mahomes’ pregnancy with baby No. 4.

The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback, 31, revealed on Wednesday, November 11, that he would ideally like to have a second baby boy, since he and son Bronze, 3, are currently outnumbered by the girls in their household.

“Obviously, it’s a blessing to have another baby on the way. I’m excited for it,” Patrick said during a team press conference. “I’m hoping that me and Bronze can even up the score.”

While the NFL player — who shares son Bronze as well as daughters Sterling, 5, and Golden, 21 months, with his wife, 31 — said he’d like to have two and two, he’s just focused on Brittany’s safety and the health of the pregnancy.

“I’m just praying for a healthy baby at the end of the day,” Patrick shared.

After a reporter pointed out that every time Patrick and Brittany have made a pregnancy announcement his team has ended their season with a Super Bowl, the athlete admitted he’d love to see that trend continue.

“I’m hoping. I don’t know if Brittany is,” Patrick said with a laugh. “But I’m hoping if we can keep that going and get another Super Bowl win with a baby on the way that’d be awesome for sure.”

Patrick and Brittany, who are high school sweethearts, announced on Tuesday, November 10, that they are expanding their brood once again.

“Another blessing from God🥹🙏🏼 & then there were 6🤍,” the pair captioned a joint Instagram post, sharing a photo of their three children lovingly touching Brittany’s stomach.

The couple welcomed their first baby, Sterling, in February 2021, after getting engaged the prior September.

After tying the knot in March 2022, Patrick and Brittany went on to welcome son Patrick “Bronze” III that November.

Their daughter Golden was born in January 2025, one month before Patrick played in his fifth Super Bowl. (The Chiefs lost to the Philadelphia Eagles during the February 2025 game, but Patrick has three championship wins to his name.)

Ahead of their fourth pregnancy announcement, both Brittany and Patrick claimed they were done having children — and happy to be a family of five.

“We’re done, we’re done for a while,” Brittany said during a June 2025 appearance on the “Whoops” podcast. “I don’t know. I mean, I feel like you can never say you’re done. I think three is all I need.”

Patrick, for his part, told reporters in July 2024 — ahead of daughter Golden’s birth — that he was “done” as well.

In January 2025, Patrick changed his tune, hinting that baby No. 4 wasn’t totally out of the question.

“My goal was always three, so we’ve had three,” he said during a Chiefs press conference. “We’ll stick there for a while and see if we need to come back and get another one later on.”

Patrick noted that “down the line” they could add another little one to their family.

The Eventide is the debut project from Studio Reset, a team made up of BioWare veterans. The game is a supernatural mystery in which player choices can affect what they find in their investigations.

Andrew Oatway, former business intelligence developer at BioWare, is working as a principal game designer on turn-based RPG Threads of Time.

Chris Hepler, a writer on Star Wars: The Old Republic, Mass Effect 2, and Mass Effect 3, is working on World of Darkness RPG Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish.

Sci-fi author Derek Kunsken was working on the now-canceled Mass Effect: Universe, and just released The Quantum Dawn, the fourth entry in his Quantum Evolution series, last week.Â

TCL has been pushing the boundaries of QLED TVs, making some of the best in the market at very competitive prices. Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. #3649. Exclusive: ‘Breaking Bad’ Star RJ Mitte, in His Own Words

For those of us who managed to land a role on Breaking Bad, the show is a formative part of our lives. It represented a chance to work on what is now considered one of the best shows TV has ever seen, and the cast and crew forged an unbreakable bond. RJ Mitte was part of the show’s heartbeat. When I spoke to him for this book, we reflected on our days shooting in New Mexico fondly.

I’ll always remember him as a young kid—bright, talented, and a real sweetheart—who was so thrilled to be on set with us that it reminded us how lucky we all were. We'll all miss him dearly. Rest in peace, RJ. —Dean Norris

The last person to join the White family was RJ Mitte, cast in the role of Walt Jr., aka “Flynn.” RJ, who was only fourteen years old at the time, joined the project after we had already begun filming the pilot, following multiple rounds of auditions stretching out over several months. You might wonder why casting Walt Jr., a comparatively minor character among the core cast, took so long. Well, it was about verisimilitude. As written, Walt Jr. had cerebral palsy, albeit a relatively minor case. It was a fundamental part of the character, and Vince was adamant that the role not be played by a nondisabled actor.

VINCE GILLIGAN, creator: I was worried at the beginning that people wouldn’t connect with Walt. They’d say, Why is this guy doing this terrible thing? And so I kind of loaded him up for bear in terms of, you know, he had a son with cerebral palsy. You felt bad for him. People bullied him.

SHARON BIALY, casting director: We had a lot of autonomy with casting, once we knew what Vince was looking for, once we all agreed that, aesthetically, we were talking about the same type of actor. A case in point is RJ Mitte’s role. Vince only wanted actors who had CP. So, we conducted a nationwide search.

RJ MITTE, Walt Jr.: Walt Jr. is actually based on a real person, a friend of Vince’s from college who had cerebral palsy. So, Vince was really particular about the role of Walt Jr. and who was going to play him.

Experienced actors who also have mild CP is not the deepest pool, of course, but there are more candidates than you might expect. And RJ Mitte’s casting has to be considered something of a surprise, given his relative lack of experience and a variety of other challenges he faced while growing up.

RJ MITTE: We were living in Houston when my sister got discovered at a water park, and that’s what brought us to LA. My sister got booked on a job at Universal Studios for an ad campaign. She was one and a half at the time. We really didn’t have a lot going on. Things were tough. My mom was a single mom, and she had recently been partially paralyzed in a car accident, and my grandparents, who I was very close to, were both sick and dying, so when we got this offer to go to LA, we took it. It was a paid trip. They put us up in a motel in Hollywood—there was a strip club on one side, and a Ralphs and a library on the other side. That’s LA.

Everything was covered for six months, so I just started acting to meet kids my own age and have a little extra cash while we were there. And it ended up turning into a career for me. I started working at a young age, not in the acting industry, but with my uncle and family jobs and stuff to make money as a young kid. I would like to think I grew up with a strong work ethic. So, when we got to LA, I hit the ground running. Within the first six months, I was on shows like Hannah Montana, Everybody Hates Chris, Weeds, Seventh Heaven, Drillbit Taylor, Epic Movie—­ all as an extra. I think that really helped prepare me for Breaking Bad, just with the quality of work and the type of professionalism that the set had. I’m very grateful, because if I did not get Breaking Bad, I wouldn’t have an acting career.

At any number of points along the journey, RJ’s dream could have died. It’s hard enough for a known actor to land a role in a show of this quality, but for a newcomer, it must have been daunting, although you never would have known it by the way he carried himself on set.

RJ MITTE: Funny story: My very first audition ever in my career was an anti­ meth campaign for the state of California. It was a wild PSA, and I ended up not getting it. A year or so later, I started auditioning for Breaking Bad. The description of the role literally said, “dark hair, big eyebrows, and mild cerebral palsy.” And I was like, that’s me!

Sharon Bialy called me in, and I already had been on quite a few auditions by that point, and I didn’t book any of them, so I knew what rejection felt like. I had a sense of, Don’t hold your breath. But I’m a firm believer that you go in owning it and when you walk out, don’t look back. Every callback was a little more like, Wait, I’m actually still in the running.

Walt Jr. had a somewhat more severe case of CP than RJ, who did not use assistive devices for mobility in real life.

RJ MITTE: When I went in for my first audition, Sharon was there, and she had hurt her foot. So, she actually handed me her crutches that she was using for the audition. Six months went by, four callbacks, four auditions, and in that final one, they’re like, Okay, we’re sending you. You’re going to New Mexico. The next day I was on a 6 a.m. flight to audition for Vince and the team. Then he excused me for a moment and brought me back in to do my test screening with Anna and Bryan.

Think about that. RJ was fourteen years old and trying to land a job that would change his life, a job that would help him support his entire family. Talk about pressure.

RJ MITTE: I think in life I’ve always had pressure. It really didn’t stand out to me too much. I can only do what I can do. And so as long as I’m doing my best, that’s what matters. But it always kind of felt like I was part of the team to some degree, even when I wasn’t. And so when it came to doing the scene with Anna and Bryan, it really felt like a family. It was like, Oh, yeah, this feels right. Apparently, they must have had the same feeling because they hired me.

Like everyone else, RJ made the most of his opportunity and crafted a fully formed portrait of an adolescent at the center of a family storm; one whose disability may have helped shape him but did not define who he was.

RJ MITTE: This was the first time I think people really saw a character with a disability who wasn’t disabled. There’s nothing he couldn’t do that other kids were doing. It wasn’t about the disability, and that’s something that I think Vince really stressed: it’s not about his disability; it’s about being a part of the family and living with it.

Five seasons in, Breaking Bad reached its apotheosis with the monumental episode “Ozymandias,” in which Walter White’s house of cards comes crashing down. It’s also the episode where Flynn learns the truth about his father’s double life, and that Walt has led my character—his brother-in-law, Hank—to his death. The episode builds to a climactic moment where Flynn’s mother, Skyler, grabs a knife and brandishes it at her husband.

RIAN JOHNSON, director, “Ozymandias”: The actual fight itself, I remember being surprisingly fun to shoot—­just making sure to give Anna and Bryan the space that they needed to find it. I think RJ also did a terrific job in that moment—­ he’s kind of the linchpin of the whole thing.

It is indeed Flynn who rises to the occasion. When Walt wrestles the knife away from Skyler, his son jumps on top of him and throws him across the room. He’s a big kid, strong enough to handle Walt despite his disability; strong enough to protect his mother.

RJ MITTE: It was very intense to shoot. At the same time, we’re professionals. Everything was very choreographed. There was one moment when we first started, I got so heated, and so into it, that I kind of accidentally grabbed Bryan the wrong way and kind of like tossed him . . . wrong. And everyone was like, “Whoa, RJ! You can’t throw him like that.” And I was like, “Oh, I’m so sorry. I just got caught up in the moment.”

RIAN JOHNSON: When you see Walt Jr. turn, then you know it’s truly over. And Bryan’s reaction to that just breaks my heart every time I see it.

In the series’s penultimate episode, Walt clandestinely calls Flynn at school. A package is on its way, he says, to be delivered to the home of one of Flynn’s friends. The package contains money, one hundred thousand dollars—­the most he could stuff into one box. “I wanted to give you so much more, but this is all I could do,” Walt explains, leaning into the pay phone as Flynn listens, wordlessly, on the other end.

RJ MITTE: I remember at the time we were shooting that scene it was in this school-slash-doctor’s-office that we were using. Bryan was in the room with me when we did this part. It definitely was heartbreaking to have to feel that way about someone that I admire. And I think that’s what Junior felt as well. I’m a believer that in life, there’s always a moment where you have to choose to either be an adult or to stay a child. This moment comes in many different forms, but it comes down to that moment where you say, Am I going to accept this and give them what they want and be submissive, and still have that child aspect of who I am? Or am I going to take charge and become the person that I need to be—­ the man, the adult?

RJ does some terrific wordless acting in this scene, wrestling with this decision. Then he speaks: “Just shut up! Just stop it. Stop it. I don’t want anything from you.”

“You need this money,” Walt says. “Your mother needs this money. It can’t all be for nothing.”

Yes, it can, as Flynn makes abundantly clear.

RJ MITTE: A lot of the decisions I made for Junior were based on my own experiences as a young adult. At the time I was still a child, but I utilized those moments from my own life of having to stand my ground and make that decision—­ realizing who I am and what I need to do to take care and provide for my family. In the show, Walt was no longer doing that. He was actually creating more danger for his family.

I think it’s very powerful that Walt Jr. had the ability to stand his ground, and to put those boundaries in place: “You’re out. This is my family now, and you’re not a part of it.” I find a lot of young men and women have to take that stance at some point, especially with parents or family figures that live in a volatile world, a world that is corrupt.

Later, in the series finale, Walt is standing over a crib, caressing the hair of baby Holly as she naps. He leaves and then watches from a distance as Flynn gets off a school bus and walks into the apartment.

VINCE GILLIGAN: With Walt, you want him to have a goodbye scene with his wife. We were sad we couldn’t have a goodbye scene with his son, Walt Jr., because RJ is a wonderful actor. We just didn’t have the room.

For those of us who were fortunate enough to be a part of it, Breaking Bad remains a seminal event in our lives, both personally and professionally—­ an opportunity to work on one of the greatest television shows in history, alongside people who became lifelong friends.

BRYAN CRANSTON: I knew when it ended that this was the role of my life.

AARON PAUL: I think I can speak for everyone involved in the show: It changed all of our lives.

RJ MITTE: I will be eighty years old in a nursing home and there will probably be someone looking at me through a window, saying, “There’s Walt Jr.” And I’m okay with that.

#3648. Pete Hegseth Publicly Scolded for Conduct at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was among a group of visitors who were publicly scolded for their disrespectful behavior during a Veterans Day event at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

A viral video showed Pete, 46, his wife, Jennifer Hegseth, and a group of aides chatting, laughing and posing for pictures at the Arlington National Cemetery monument on Wednesday, November 11, moments after an annual Veteran’s Day commemoration ceremony concluded. (As part of the memorial ceremony, President Donald Trump laid a wreath at the tomb to honor fallen troops.)

A laugh could be heard from someone in Hegseth’s group seconds before a U.S. Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier loudly and sternly reminded them of proper conduct.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the soldier shouted.

Hegseth looked back over his shoulder toward the Army guard who reprimanded them before continuing on with the rest of his group.

Proper protocol while visiting the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is to remain completely silent in deference to those who have fallen in service of the country.

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told Us later on Wednesday that Hegseth and his staff “have always honored and will always honor” the sacrifices of service members.

“While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum,” Parnell added.

Wednesday’s incident compounded more than a week of unflattering headlines for Hegseth. Retiring Rep. Thomas Massie, of Kentucky, introduced updated articles of impeachment against Hegseth in the House of Representatives on Monday, November 9, accusing the Secretary of Defense of committing “high crimes and misdemeanors” for not seeking Congress’ approval to launch military action in Iran this past February.

Hegseth defended his conduct at a Tuesday, November 10, press conference, insisting that “no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations.”

“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth alleged. “This is sabotage.”

House Republicans used the waning days of their majority to officially table Massie’s resolution, thereby sending it to committee rather than compelling a floor vote. Articles of impeachment against Hegseth could be revisited by Democrats in the House when they begin a new session of Congress with a significant majority on January 3, 2027.

Prior to the impeachment controversy, Washington, D.C., insiders pointed to a potential rift between Hegseth and Vice President JD Vance after Vance, 42, placed the blame for Democrats’ landslide midterm victory on a growing dissatisfaction among the U.S. populace with the War in Iran.

“If you’d like to argue [the war] was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Vance wrote via X on November 4. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Hegseth held his first Pentagon briefing in nearly 190 days on Tuesday, in which he insisted that he “respect[s] the vice president greatly.”

“I’m certainly not going to exchange in any finger-pointing, and thankfully, politics is not really my thing,” the former Fox News weekend political host insisted. “I do the Department of War and making sure we’re prepared and ready.”

Hegseth went on to say, “A lot of people are going to look at the conflict and assess it, and the vice president has been a critical member of the team in every aspect of this, and we’re grateful for all the input he’s given me personally and our department.”

#3647. Nintendo’s Latest Volley Of DMCA Takedowns Wipes Over 200 Nintendo Switch Projects Off Of GitHub

Nintendoâs famously…efficient lawyers have issued GitHub four DMCA notices over the last week, effectively wiping roughly 217 Nintendo Switch-related repositories and forks (alternative versions of the console’s source code) from the site. However, while three of the four DMCA notices targeted repositories for Switch emulators, the largest one appears to be a first for Nintendo: a legal takedown notice for the firmware of a Nintendo Switch modchip named Picofly, a chip that can be soldered onto the console and used to bypass security checks.

As first reported by TorrentFreak, the latest wave of Nintendo GitHub DMCA notices appeared on the site on November 9. Three of the four notices are for Nintendoâs old nemesis, Yuzu, the Nintendo Switch emulator created by Tropic Haze LLC, which agreed to pay Nintendo $2.4 million in damages back in 2024.Â One of these three targeted Citron Neo, which is a fork of the Yuzu emulator. The Citron Neo DMCA notice wiped 71 repositories from GitHub in one fell swoop. Nintendo justified the legal notice by referencing the same âNintendo of America Inc. v. Tropic Haze LLCâ case that led to Yuzu being taken offline.

This is par for the course as far as Nintendoâs litigious history is concerned, which is why the final DMCA notice is arguably a lot more interesting. As TorrentFreak notes, the notice for the Picofly GitHub repo specifically targets firmware for Nintendo Switch modchips; the software that allows said modchips to run unauthorised programs.

Picofly is a âcompatible alternativeâ to the SX Core and SX Lite modchips; the same modchips that landed Team Xecuterâs Gary Bowser (no relation) in jail for 40 months back in 2022. According to the takedown notice, Nintendo justified the Picofly firmware massacre on GitHub as the repos contain the same âtechnological protection measures that permit the Nintendo Switch console to interact only with legitimate Nintendo video game files.â

Nintendoâs November 9 DMCA notices donât appear to be related to the vibe-coded Switch ports that exploded onto GitHub over the past two months.

#3645. These Sony ANC Headphones Are on Sale for $128 Right Now

It's hard to convince yourself to spend nearly half a grand on premium headphones, like the Sony WH-1000XM6, even if you consider yourself an audiophile. Not everyone can afford those prices, which is why the budget, mid-tier, and premium tiers exist. While the premium 1000XM6 headphones are over three times the price of the mid-tier Sony WH-CH730N, they're not three times as good. The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179) right now, the lowest price they've ever been according to price-tracking tools, and they offer an amazing value for your money.

It's pretty impressive what $128 in headphones gets you in 2026. The CH730N uses the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0. The Adaptive Sound Control feature can detect your activity (walking, sitting down, loud environment, etc.) and automatically switch the level of ANC and transparency to make your experience as comfortable and seamless as possible.

The microphones are decent and use a feature to isolate your voice in noisy environments. I love that there's an AUX connection to give you the option, which seems to be coming back with newer headphones. The design is light and will feel like plastic, but they are comfortable to wear for long sessions. If you're looking to maximize the quality of headphones you can get for your money, the Sony WH-CH730N offer a pretty compelling option at $128.

#3644. Kirk Cousins Reveals Kids' Reaction to News He Was Traded Back to Vikings

Kirk Cousins and his wife Julie‘s two sons are embracing their family’s big move following the quarterback’s trade from the Las Vegas Raiders back to the Minnesota Vikings.

“[The kids] are ready and excited for the next several weeks,” Kirk, 38, beamed during his first press conference as a Viking on Wednesday, November 11.

The Vikings acquired Kirk from the Raiders in exchange for a third-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft in a deal that went down to the wire before the Tuesday, November 10, trade deadline. Cousins previously played for the Vikings from 2018 through 2023 before moving to the Atlanta Falcons from 2024 to 2025.

Kirk’s’ single season with the Raiders in 2026 saw him starting in all nine games thus far, defying most analysts’ expectations regarding his performance.

During Wednesday’s media scrum, Kirk relayed how Jennifer had broken the news to their sons, Cooper, 9, and Turner, 7, about their dad’s big NFL trade.

“I was hoping they were going to come with me [to Minnesota], but I said, ‘What are you thinking, Julie?’ It was her call. And she said, ‘I don’t think we can pull the boys out of school and baseball and their friends,'” he recalled.

The athlete continued, “[Julie] picked them up from school and told them, ‘Here’s the situation: Dad got traded to the Minnesota Vikings. What would you guys want to do?’ They looked at her and they said, ‘Let’s go.'”

Julie previously commemorated her family’s move to the Twin Cities via her Instagram Story on Tuesday, writing, “Another adventure awaits…”

She shared that her son Turner had one important stop to make before the family headed to the airport.

“1 hour before we leave for Minnesota…Turner wanted one last at bat in his little league playoff game 😍,” Julie revealed via her Story. “We love you, Las Vegas!”

Kirk opened up to the media about how he learned about the trade, joking that he was “about halfway into my eggs” on Tuesday morning when he received an unexpected call from Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak.

“I looked at my teammates and said, ‘I have a guess what this might mean.’ Although, he calls on occasion,” Kirk explained. “[Kubiak] said, ‘Are you in the building?’ I said, ‘I am.’ He said, ‘Why don’t you come up?’ And my heart started beating a little faster.”

Kirk was told about the particulars of the trade during a private meeting with Kubiak, 39, and Raiders general manager John Spytek. He also connected with Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell on the phone before the deal was completed.

“Kevin knows me. Kevin knows what I do well,” Kirk noted. “Kevin knows what I don’t do well. Kevin knows what I can handle. Kevin knows what I can’t handle. And I think that helps. Not just that he knows your strengths, but that he knows your weaknesses — and that as a result, he’s going to try to protect you and not have you do things that he knows, ‘You know what? That’s not how Kirk functions. That’s not his best chance of success.'”

Kirk added, “I think the fact [Kevin] knows me well, the good about me and the bad about me, I think that should help us.”

Fox airs live coverage on Sunday, November 15, as the Vikings head to the historic Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin, to face the Green Bay Packers.

Jensen Huang founded Nvidia back in 1993 and called each of the company’s major shots along the way, from its focus on gaming graphics to its latest pivot to AI. He’s now resigned as CEO following reports of multiple affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

“Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately,” reads a new press release from the tech giant on November 12. “Jensenâs contributions to Nvidia are profound,” the press release stated. “Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”

#3642. This Samsung 32-Inch OLED Gaming Monitor Is $300 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.
